questions.stem:
With reference to the Parliament of India, consider the following statements :
1. A private member's bill is a bill presented by a Member of Parliament who is not elected but only nominated by the President of India.
2. Recently, a private member's bill has been passed in the Parliament of India for the first time in its history.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Neither statement is correct.**

- **St. 1 — wrong.** A *private member* is **any MP who is not a Minister**, elected or nominated. The distinction is minister vs non-minister, not elected vs nominated. Private members' bills are taken up on Friday afternoons.
- **St. 2 — wrong.** It is **not** the first time: **14 private members' bills have been passed** by Parliament since 1952, the last one in **1970** (Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Bill, 1968). The 2015 Rights of Transgender Persons Bill (Tiruchi Siva) passed only the **Rajya Sabha**, not Parliament.

questions.stem:
With reference to the difference between the culture of Rigvedic Aryans and Indus Valley people, which of the following statements is/are correct ?
1. Rigvedic Aryans used the coat of mail and helmet in warfare whereas the people of Indus Valley Civilization did not leave any evidence of using them.
2. Rigvedic Aryans knew gold, silver and copper whereas Indus Valley people knew only copper and iron.
3. Rigvedic Aryans had domesticated the horse whereas there is no evidence of Indus Valley people having been aware of this animal.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**Answer: (c) 1 and 3 only.** Statement 2 kills itself; the whole question is a referendum on statement 3.

- **(1) True.** The Rigveda names both items directly — *varman* (coat of mail) and *śipra* (helmet), alongside *hiranyakaśipu*, the metal body-armour of the chariot-fighter. No Harappan site has produced armour or a helmet. Standard texts make exactly this contrast, and this statement is lifted almost verbatim from that line. Keep it.

- **(2) False — and it is the statement the question is built on.** Two independent errors in seven words. First, the Harappans certainly knew **gold and silver**: gold beads, fillets and the silver vessels and ornaments from Mohenjo-daro, Allahdino and Kunal are among the best-known Harappan finds — so "**only** copper and iron" is false on the quantifier alone. Second, and fatally, **the Harappans had no iron**. The Mature Harappan is a **Bronze Age** culture (c. 2600–1900 BCE); iron appears in the subcontinent only around c. 1200–1000 BCE with the Painted Grey Ware horizon. The statement is anachronistic by roughly seven centuries. Strike 2 — and with it, options **(b)** and **(d)**.

- **(3) True, as the exam means it.** The Rigveda is saturated with the horse — *aśva*, the chariot (*ratha*), the *aśvamedha*; the domesticated horse is the defining animal of Rigvedic material culture. On the Harappan side, the horse is absent from the **entire seal corpus** — thousands of seals show the humped bull, buffalo, elephant, rhinoceros, tiger, goat and the composite unicorn, and never once the horse — and it is absent from the accepted faunal record of the mature phase.

**Why (a) "1 only" is the trap, and why it fails.** Choosing (a) means rejecting 3 on the strength of the **Surkotada bones** (Bökönyi, 1993) and stray claims from Lothal and Kalibangan. But those finds are precisely what the standard position rejects: **Meadow and Patel re-identified them as *Equus hemionus khur*, the wild half-ass (onager)** — a different animal — and even on Bökönyi's own reading the bones are few, stray and from the terminal levels. A **contested species identification in a single excavation report is not "evidence of awareness"**; it is an open archaeological dispute. UPSC sets from the settled textbook line, which states flatly that the Harappans did not know the horse.

**The word that decides it.** Statement 3's spine is "*had domesticated the horse*". The solver read the second clause — "no evidence of... having been aware of this animal" — as a claim that not one horse bone exists anywhere in the Indus zone, then produced Surkotada to refute it. That is the wrong axis. The contrast being drawn is between a **horse-centred, chariot-using culture** and one whose iconography, faunal record and technology show no domesticated horse at all. On that reading — the only reading the standard sources support — 3 is correct.

**Note on the absolutes heuristic.** "No evidence" normally smells like a false statement, and in most Prelims sets you would strike it. This is the exception: here the absolute is the textbook's own formulation, not the setter's exaggeration. Compare it with 2, where the absolute ("**only** copper and iron") is the setter's planted error. Same word-shape, opposite verdicts — the test is whether the source itself states the absolute.

**Exam-hall rule:** when one statement is a plain textbook line and the other rests on a disputed excavation report, mark the textbook line. Elimination alone gets you most of the way — 2 is dead on iron, so it is (a) or (c), and 3 decides it. **(c).**
questions.tagging_note: Comparison question spanning IVC and the Rigvedic period equally. Primary set to ANM-01 because the discriminating facts (no horse evidence, copper but not iron) are Harappan facts; ANM-02 is genuinely co-tested.
questions.review_flag: Official key says c, worked solution said a (high confidence).

questions.stem: 'Recognition of Prior Learning Scheme' is sometimes mentioned in the news with reference to
options: Certifying the skills acquired by construction workers through traditional channels.
Enrolling the persons in Universities for distance learning programmes.
Reserving some skilled jobs to rural and urban poor in some public sector undertakings.
Certifying the skills acquired by trainees under the National Skill Development Programme.
questions.explanation_md:
**RPL certifies skills people already picked up informally — it does not train them.**

Recognition of Prior Learning is a component of **PMKVY** under the Ministry of Skill Development & Entrepreneurship, which assesses and certifies workers who learned on the job or through **traditional/family channels**, aligning them to the **NSQF** so they get formal recognition, a certificate and better wages. It was pushed hardest in the **construction sector** (with CREDAI/NSDC and the Construction Skill Development Council).

Option (d) is the trap: **trainees under a skill-development programme get ordinary training certification, not RPL** — RPL exists precisely for those who never entered formal training.
questions.tagging_note: Recognition of Prior Learning sits under PMKVY/NSDC skilling. Straddles CA schemes tracker and the employment/skilling side of ECO-17; there is no dedicated skill-development topic in the vocabulary.

questions.stem: From the ecological point of view, which one of the following assumes importance in being a good link between the Eastern Ghats and the Western Ghats ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve (Erode, Tamil Nadu) is the ecological bridge between the Eastern and Western Ghats.**

It sits in the **Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve** and connects the Western Ghats (via Mudumalai–Bandipur–BRT) with the Eastern Ghats hills, making it a critical **elephant and tiger corridor**. Declared a tiger reserve in 2013.

The others are all wholly on one side: **Nallamala** and **Seshachalam** lie entirely in the **Eastern Ghats** (Andhra Pradesh), **Nagarhole** entirely in the **Western Ghats** (Karnataka).
questions.tagging_note: Tests a specific tiger reserve as an Eastern–Western Ghats corridor. Protected areas (ENV-06) is the best fit; wildlife corridor/connectivity as a concept is not separately listed, so ENV-05 carries the biodiversity-linkage element.

questions.stem: One of the implications of equality in society is the absence of
questions.explanation_md:
**Equality means the absence of special privileges.**

Equality does not abolish restraints (law restrains everyone equally), competition (equality of opportunity presumes it), or ideology. What it removes is **birth-, class- or rank-based privilege** — mirrored in **Art. 14–18**, especially **Art. 18 (abolition of titles)** and Art. 15/16 (no discrimination in access to public offices).
questions.tagging_note: GAP: this is an abstract political-theory question (the concept of equality), not constitutional law. No topic in the vocabulary covers political theory / political concepts. POL-07 (Right to Equality, incl. abolition of titles and privileges) is the nearest anchor but is a genuine stretch.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements in respect of Trade Related Analysis of Fauna and Flora in Commerce (TRAFFIC) :
1. TRAFFIC is a bureau under United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP).
2. The mission of TRAFFIC is to ensure that trade in wild plants and animals is not a threat to the conservation of nature.
Which of the above statements is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Only statement 2 is correct.**

- **St. 1 — wrong.** TRAFFIC is **not a UN body**. It is a **joint programme of WWF and IUCN**, founded in 1976, headquartered in Cambridge, UK. It works closely with the CITES Secretariat but is an NGO network.
- **St. 2 — correct.** Its stated mission is to ensure that **trade in wild plants and animals is not a threat to the conservation of nature**. TRAFFIC India operates as a division of WWF-India.
questions.tagging_note: TRAFFIC is a WWF–IUCN joint programme (not UNEP) working on wildlife trade, i.e. the CITES space. The vocabulary has no topic for international environmental organisations/NGOs — ENV-10 covers Indian institutions only — so ENV-14 (conventions incl. CITES) is the closest available fit.
questions.transcription_note: Statement 2 carries the negative 'not', printed as plain text (no emphasis). The scan of the lead-in renders as 'is/arc correct' due to a print/scan artifact for 'is/are correct'; transcribed as 'is/are correct'.

questions.stem: Which principle among the following was added to the Directive Principles of State Policy by the 42nd Amendment to the Constitution ?
options: Equal pay for equal work for both men and women
Participation of workers in the management of industries
Right to work, education and public assistance
Securing living wage and human conditions of work to workers
questions.explanation_md:
**The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Article 43A — participation of workers in the management of industries.**

The 42nd Amendment inserted **three** new DPSPs: **39A** (equal justice and free legal aid), **43A** (workers' participation in management), **48A** (protection of environment, forests and wildlife). It also amended Art. 39(f).

The rest are original 1950 provisions: **equal pay for equal work — Art. 39(d)**; right to work/education/public assistance — Art. 41; living wage and humane conditions of work — Art. 43. (Note: Art. 38(2), on reducing inequalities, came via the **44th** Amendment, 1978.)

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements is correct ?
options: Rights are claims of the State against the citizens.
Rights are privileges which are incorporated in the Constitution of a State.
Rights are claims of the citizens against the State.
Rights are privileges of a few citizens against the many.
questions.explanation_md:
**Rights are claims of the citizens against the State.**

A right is a claim recognised by society and enforceable **against the State**, which has the corresponding duty to protect it — this is exactly the logic of **Art. 12–13**, where "State" is defined and any law violating Fundamental Rights is void, and of **Art. 32**, the citizen's remedy against the State.

Why the others fail: rights are not the State's claims on citizens (those are *duties*); they are not mere constitutional grants (natural/moral rights exist before codification); and privileges of a few over the many are the **opposite** of rights, which are universal.
questions.tagging_note: GAP: another abstract political-theory question (nature of rights vis-a-vis the State), not a Constitution-article question. No political-theory topic exists in the vocabulary; POL-07 is used because Art 12 defines 'the State' against which rights are claimed, but the fit is weak. Q5 and Q8 together indicate a missing 'political theory / basic concepts' node.

questions.stem: Which of the following gives 'Global Gender Gap Index' ranking to the countries of the world ?
questions.explanation_md:
**The Global Gender Gap Index is published by the World Economic Forum (WEF), Geneva — since 2006.**

It ranks countries on four sub-indices: **economic participation and opportunity, educational attainment, health and survival, and political empowerment**. It measures *gaps* between men and women, not absolute levels of development.

Don't confuse it with the **Gender Inequality Index / Gender Development Index (UNDP)**. Other WEF reports worth remembering: Global Competitiveness Report, Global Risks Report, Energy Transition Index, Travel & Tourism Development Index.

questions.stem:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding Smart India Hackathon 2017 ?
1. It is a centrally sponsored scheme for developing every city of our country into Smart Cities in a decade.
2. It is an initiative to identify new digital technology innovations for solving the many problems faced by our country.
3. It is a programme aimed at making all the financial transactions in our country completely digital in a decade.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**Only statement 2 is correct.**

Smart India Hackathon 2017 was a **nationwide product-development competition** run by MHRD, AICTE, i4c, Persistent Systems and Rambhau Mhalgi Prabodhini, in which student teams built **digital/software solutions to problems posed by central ministries and departments**. It was a 36-hour non-stop coding event, not a scheme.

- **St. 1 — wrong.** Urban development of cities is the **Smart Cities Mission** — a different programme entirely; the word "Smart" is the trap.
- **St. 3 — wrong.** Full digitisation of financial transactions relates to **Digital India / cashless economy pushes (BHIM, DigiDhan)**, not the hackathon.
questions.tagging_note: Smart India Hackathon is a government initiative for crowdsourcing digital innovation; it straddles the schemes tracker (CAI-10) and S&T policy/missions (SNT-14). The distractors also invoke Smart Cities and digital payments, but the question does not actually test those topics.

questions.stem:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) ?
1. It decides the RBI's benchmark interest rates.
2. It is a 12-member body including the Governor of RBI and is reconstituted every year.
3. It functions under the chairmanship of the Union Finance Minister.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**1 — correct.** The MPC fixes the policy repo rate, RBI's benchmark rate, to meet the 4% (+/- 2%) CPI inflation target.

**2 — wrong. The MPC has 6 members, not 12** — 3 from RBI (Governor as chair, Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer) and 3 appointed by the Centre for a **4-year non-renewable term** (so not reconstituted every year).

**3 — wrong.** Chaired by the **RBI Governor**, who also holds the casting vote in a tie. The Finance Minister has no seat.

Only 1 stands. Statutory basis: RBI Act amendment, 2016.

questions.stem:
With reference to Manipuri Sankirtana, consider the following statements :
1. It is a song and dance performance.
2. Cymbals are the only musical instruments used in the performance.
3. It is performed to narrate the life and deeds of Lord Krishna.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
Manipuri Sankirtana was inscribed on **UNESCO's Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2013**.

**1 — correct.** It is ritual singing, drumming and dancing performed in the Vaishnava temple (mandap) and at life-cycle events.

**2 — wrong. The pung (barrel drum) is the central instrument**, played by dancing drummers; cymbals (kartal/mandila) accompany it. "Only cymbals" kills the statement — an "only" word almost always does.

**3 — correct.** The content is the life and deeds of Krishna, in the Gaudiya Vaishnava tradition brought to Manipur under Raja Bhagyachandra (18th c.).

So 1 and 3.
questions.tagging_note: Manipuri Sankirtana is a composite ritual form — statement 1 tests it as song-and-dance (ART-07) and statement 2 tests the instruments used, pung drum plus cymbals (ART-08).

questions.stem:
Who among the following was/were associated with the introduction of Ryotwari Settlement in India during the British rule ?
1. Lord Cornwallis
2. Alexander Read
3. Thomas Munro
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**Cornwallis = Permanent Settlement (Bengal, 1793)** — zamindari, not ryotwari. That single fact eliminates every option containing 1, leaving only (c).

**Alexander Read** first tried the ryotwari experiment in the **Baramahal** district ceded after the Third Anglo-Mysore War (1792).

**Thomas Munro**, Read's assistant there, extended it to the ceded districts and, as Governor of Madras (1820–27), made it the system for the Madras Presidency.

Ryotwari = settlement made **directly with the individual cultivator (ryot)**, no intermediary, revenue revised periodically (usually 30 years).

questions.stem:
In the context of solving pollution problems, what is/are the advantage/advantages of bioremediation technique ?
1. It is a technique for cleaning up pollution by enhancing the same biodegradation process that occurs in nature.
2. Any contaminant with heavy metals such as cadmium and lead can be readily and completely treated by bioremediation using microorganisms.
3. Genetic engineering can be used to create microorganisms specifically designed for bioremediation.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**1 — correct.** Bioremediation simply speeds up the natural microbial breakdown of contaminants (adding nutrients, oxygen, or moisture = biostimulation).

**2 — wrong. Heavy metals such as cadmium and lead are elements — they cannot be biodegraded at all.** Microbes can only immobilise, sequester or change their oxidation state (bio-sorption / bio-transformation). "Readily and completely treated" is false.

**3 — correct.** Genetically engineered microbes (the classic case being Ananda Chakrabarty's oil-degrading *Pseudomonas*) are designed for specific pollutants.

So 1 and 3.
questions.tagging_note: Straddles subjects: the frame is pollution remediation (ENV-11) but statement 3 turns on genetically engineered microorganisms (SNT-03).

questions.stem: The Trade Disputes Act of 1929 provided for
options: the participation of workers in the management of industries.
arbitrary powers to the management to quell industrial disputes.
an intervention by the British Court in the event of a trade dispute.
a system of tribunals and a ban on strikes.
questions.explanation_md:
The **Trade Disputes Act, 1929** set up machinery for settling disputes — **Courts of Inquiry and Boards of Conciliation (a tribunal system)** — and **banned strikes and lockouts in public utility services** without notice, plus strikes with political/coercive objects.

It is the immediate backdrop to the **Meerut Conspiracy Case (1929)** and the protests against it in the Central Legislative Assembly; Bhagat Singh and B.K. Dutt threw the bomb in the Assembly on **8 April 1929** while this Bill and the Public Safety Bill were being pushed through.

Nothing in it gave workers a role in management (rules out a), and no British court intervention was created (rules out c).
questions.tagging_note: The Trade Disputes Act 1929 sits in the labour-movement material (HIS-15) but is usually read alongside the 1928-29 repressive legislation of the Simon/Civil Disobedience years (HIS-11). No topic in the tree is specifically about colonial labour legislation.

questions.stem: Local self-government can be best explained as an exercise in
questions.explanation_md:
**Local self-government = democratic decentralisation**: power is transferred to *elected* bodies (panchayats, municipalities) that are accountable to the local electorate, not merely to a superior office.

Why not the others:
- **Federalism** is the division of power between Union and States; local bodies are creatures of State law, not a third federal tier in the classical sense.
- **Administrative delegation** means an official passes duties to a subordinate — no election, no autonomy. Decentralisation to elected bodies is the opposite.
- **Direct democracy** is citizens deciding themselves (Gram Sabha is one element, but the *institution* is representative).

Basis: 73rd and 74th Amendments, 1992.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
With reference to the Constitution of India, the Directive Principles of State Policy constitute limitations upon
1. legislative function.
2. executive function.
Which of the above statements is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**The load-bearing word is "limitations" — a term of art, not a loose synonym for "applies to".**

In constitutional law a *limitation* is a boundary whose breach a court will enforce: cross it and the law or the act is void. Part III does exactly that — Article 13 declares any law inconsistent with the Fundamental Rights void to the extent of the inconsistency, and the rights are phrased as negative injunctions ("the State shall not..."). **That** is a limitation upon legislative and executive function.

Part IV is built the opposite way round.

- **Article 37** — the Directive Principles "shall not be enforceable by any court", but "it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws." A duty to act, expressly stripped of judicial enforceability.
- **No law has ever been struck down for violating a DPSP**, and none can be. No executive order can be quashed for contravening one. If breaching a provision voids nothing, that provision limits nothing.
- **Article 31C points the other way entirely.** A law giving effect to Article 39(b) or (c) is shielded from challenge under Articles 14 and 19. There the DPSP *enlarge* legislative power at the expense of the Fundamental Rights. A genuine limitation cannot expand the power it supposedly limits.

So: **(1) False. (2) False. Answer (d).**

**Why (c) is the trap.** Both statements *sound* right because DPSP are addressed to "the State" under Article 12 — which does cover legislature and executive — and Article 37 does put a duty on both. The candidate reads "DPSP bear upon legislative and executive function" (true) and ticks Both. But the stem does not say *bear upon*, *guide*, or *direct*. It says **constitute limitations upon**. Directing is positive and unenforceable; limiting is negative and justiciable. Part IV is a mandate to move in a direction, not a fence you cannot cross.

**Carry this pair:** Fundamental Rights *limit* the State; Directive Principles *direct* it. Any question that swaps one verb for the other is testing exactly that swap.
questions.review_flag: Official key says d, worked solution said c (medium confidence).

questions.stem: The term 'Digital Single Market Strategy' seen in the news refers to
questions.explanation_md:
The **Digital Single Market Strategy is the European Union's**, launched in **May 2015** by the European Commission.

Three pillars: better access to online goods and services across borders, the right conditions for digital networks, and maximising the growth potential of the digital economy.

Its most visible outputs are the **end of mobile roaming charges (June 2017)**, the **ban on unjustified geo-blocking**, portability of online content, and the data-protection/e-commerce rules that sit alongside GDPR.

Memory hook: "Single Market" is EU vocabulary — ASEAN, BRICS and G20 do not have one.
questions.tagging_note: A terms-in-news question about an internal EU policy strategy, not about India-EU relations. CAI-02 is the only topic that carries the EU; the tree has no bucket for standalone 'terms in the news' outside the India-centric IR topics.

questions.stem: At one of the places in India, if you stand on the seashore and watch the sea, you will find that the sea water recedes from the shore line a few kilometres and comes back to the shore, twice a day, and you can actually walk on the sea floor when the water recedes. This unique phenomenon is seen at
questions.explanation_md:
**Chandipur, Balasore district, Odisha** — the "hide-and-seek beach". The sea withdraws up to **about 5 km at low tide, twice a day**, exposing the seabed for people to walk on, then returns.

Cause: an exceptionally **gentle, shallow gradient of the shore combined with a high tidal range** at the head of the Bay of Bengal near the Budhabalanga river mouth.

Also the site of the **Integrated Test Range (ITR)** for India's missile tests — the same place, useful for a second question.

Bhavnagar (Gujarat) has a large tidal range but no such walking-out phenomenon; Bheemunipatnam (AP) and Nagapattinam (TN) do not.
questions.tagging_note: Location-identification from a described phenomenon (Chandipur's receding tide). Tests place knowledge (GEO-24) resting on tides (GEO-10) and the Indian coast (GEO-12); format could equally be read as simple since the options are four plain place names.

questions.stem:
With reference to the 'Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988 (PBPT Act)', consider the following statements :
1. A property transaction is not treated as a benami transaction if the owner of the property is not aware of the transaction.
2. Properties held benami are liable for confiscation by the Government.
3. The Act provides for three authorities for investigations but does not provide for any appellate mechanism.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**1 — wrong, and it is the exact reverse of the Act.** The definition of a benami transaction expressly *includes* a transaction where **the owner of the property is not aware of, or denies knowledge of, such ownership** (also: property held in a fictitious name, or where the person providing the consideration is untraceable).

**2 — correct.** Property held benami is **liable to confiscation by the Central Government without any compensation**. Penalty: rigorous imprisonment 1–7 years plus a fine up to 25% of fair market value.

**3 — wrong on both halves.** The Act provides **four** authorities — Initiating Officer, Approving Authority, Administrator, Adjudicating Authority — and it **does** provide an appellate mechanism: an **Appellate Tribunal**, with further appeal to the High Court.

Only 2 stands. (The 1988 Act was given teeth by the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016, in force 1 Nov 2016.)
questions.tagging_note: Gap in the vocabulary: no topic covers black-money / benami law or its adjudicating and appellate machinery. ECO-11 (taxation) is the nearest fit because the PBPT Act is administered by the income-tax authorities; POL-27 governance was considered and rejected as a worse fit.
questions.transcription_note: Three negatives ('not' twice in statement 1, 'does not' in statement 3) are printed as plain text with no emphasis; all verified present against the scan.

questions.stem:
Due to some reasons, if there is a huge fall in the population of species of butterflies, what could be its likely consequence/consequences ?
1. Pollination of some plants could be adversely affected.
2. There could be a drastic increase in the fungal infections of some cultivated plants.
3. It could lead to a fall in the population of some species of wasps, spiders and birds.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**Butterflies are pollinators and prey — not fungal controls.**

- **(1) Correct.** Butterflies are important pollinators for many wild and cultivated flowering plants (especially long-tubed, brightly coloured, day-blooming flowers). Fewer butterflies → poorer pollination.
- **(2) Wrong.** Butterflies have no role in suppressing fungi. If anything, caterpillar feeding *wounds* plants and opens entry points for fungal pathogens — so fewer butterflies would, if anything, **reduce** fungal infection, not cause a "drastic increase".
- **(3) Correct.** Butterflies and their caterpillars are food for insectivorous birds and spiders, and caterpillars are hosts for parasitoid wasps. Removing a prey/host base pulls those predator and parasitoid populations down — a classic trophic cascade.

So 1 and 3 only → **(c)**.

questions.stem:
It is possible to produce algae based biofuels, but what is/are the likely limitation(s) of developing countries in promoting this industry ?
1. Production of algae based biofuels is possible in seas only and not on continents.
2. Setting up and engineering the algae based biofuel production requires high level of expertise/technology until the construction is completed.
3. Economically viable production necessitates the setting up of large scale facilities which may raise ecological and social concerns.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**Statement 1 is the giveaway — algae biofuel is mostly a *land*-based industry.**

- **(1) Wrong.** Algae are cultivated in **open raceway ponds and closed photobioreactors on land**, using freshwater, brackish or waste water. Sea-based cultivation is one option, not the only one. The word "only" kills it.
- **(2) Correct.** Strain selection, photobioreactor design, harvesting and lipid extraction need advanced engineering and skilled manpower — a genuine constraint for developing countries.
- **(3) Correct.** Economies of scale demand very large facilities → large land/water footprint, competition for land and water with agriculture and settlements → ecological and social objections.

2 and 3 only → **(b)**.
questions.tagging_note: Algae biofuel sits in ENV-16 (biofuels and national missions); the scale/expertise angle also touches SNT-12 energy technology.

questions.stem:
Which of the following are the objectives of 'National Nutrition Mission' ?
1. To create awareness relating to malnutrition among pregnant women and lactating mothers.
2. To reduce the incidence of anaemia among young children, adolescent girls and women.
3. To promote the consumption of millets, coarse cereals and unpolished rice.
4. To promote the consumption of poultry eggs.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**NNM targets outcomes (stunting, undernutrition, anaemia, low birth weight) — not particular foods.**

- **(1) Correct.** Awareness generation and behaviour-change communication for pregnant women and lactating mothers is a core NNM component.
- **(2) Correct.** **Reducing anaemia among young children, adolescent girls and women is an explicit NNM target** (anaemia reduction by 3% per annum in the mission's stated goals).
- **(3) Wrong.** Promoting millets/coarse cereals/unpolished rice is not a stated NNM objective — that belongs to food-security and millet-promotion programmes.
- **(4) Wrong.** Egg promotion is a State-level mid-day-meal/ICDS menu decision, not an NNM objective.

1 and 2 only → **(a)**.
questions.tagging_note: National Nutrition Mission is a scheme (CAI-10 schemes tracker) but the substance is nutrition/health indicators (ECO-18). No topic in the tree covers nutrition/malnutrition specifically.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. The Factories Act, 1881 was passed with a view to fix the wages of industrial workers and to allow the workers to form trade unions.
2. N.M. Lokhande was a pioneer in organizing the labour movement in British India.
Which of the above statements is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**The Factories Act, 1881 was about child labour and machine safety — not wages, not unions.**

- **(1) Wrong.** The 1881 Act prohibited employment of children below **7 years**, capped children aged 7–12 at **9 hours a day**, gave four monthly holidays, and required fencing of dangerous machinery. It said nothing about wages, and trade unions were legalised only much later (**Trade Unions Act, 1926**).
- **(2) Correct.** **Narayan Meghaji Lokhande**, a Jyotiba Phule associate, founded the **Bombay Mill-Hands Association (1884)** — the first Indian labour organisation — and edited *Dinabandhu*. He is rightly called the pioneer of the labour movement in British India.

Only 2 → **(b)**.
questions.tagging_note: Lokhande and the Factories Act belong to the labour movement strand of HIS-15; the Factories Act itself is also a British economic/industrial policy item (HIS-02).

questions.stem:
In the context of mitigating the impending global warming due to anthropogenic emissions of carbon dioxide, which of the following can be the potential sites for carbon sequestration ?
1. Abandoned and uneconomic coal seams
2. Depleted oil and gas reservoirs
3. Subterranean deep saline formations
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**All three are standard geological CO₂ storage reservoirs.**

- **(1) Correct.** Unmineable/abandoned coal seams — CO₂ adsorbs onto coal and can displace methane (enhanced coal-bed methane recovery).
- **(2) Correct.** Depleted oil and gas reservoirs — proven trap geology (they held hydrocarbons for millions of years) and existing well infrastructure; also used for enhanced oil recovery.
- **(3) Correct.** **Deep saline aquifers are the largest-capacity option worldwide** — porous rock filled with non-potable brine, e.g. the Sleipner project in the North Sea.

All three → **(d)**. Rule of thumb: any deep, porous, well-capped formation that is not a drinking-water source is a candidate.
questions.tagging_note: Geological carbon sequestration (CCS) is not named explicitly anywhere in the tree; ENV-12 climate change science is the closest genuine home.

questions.stem: The object of the Butler Committee of 1927 was to
options: Define the jurisdiction of the Central and Provincial Governments.
Define the powers of the Secretary of State for India.
Improve the relationship between the Government of India and the Indian States.
questions.explanation_md:
**Butler Committee = Indian States Committee = princely states.**

Appointed in **1927 under Sir Harcourt Butler** to examine the relationship between the **Paramount Power (Crown) and the Indian princely states**. It reported in 1929 that paramountcy must remain paramount, that the states' relationship was with the Crown and not with a future responsible Indian government, and that states should not be transferred to an Indian government without their consent.

So the object was to **improve/define relations between the Government of India and the Indian States → (d)**. Not to be confused with the Simon Commission (also 1927, but on constitutional reform).
questions.tagging_note: Butler Committee 1927 (Crown–princely states relations) is not named in the tree. Placed in HIS-11 on chronology (Simon Commission era); HIS-09 constitutional developments is the alternative. Princely states / integration is a genuine gap in the vocabulary.

questions.stem: The term 'Domestic Content Requirement' is sometimes seen in the news with reference to
options: Developing solar power production in our country
Granting licences to foreign T.V. channels in our country
Exporting our food products to other countries
Permitting foreign educational institutions to set up their campuses in our country
questions.explanation_md:
**DCR = solar.**

Under the **Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission**, a share of capacity was reserved for developers who used **domestically manufactured solar cells and modules** — the Domestic Content Requirement.

The **USA challenged it at the WTO and won (2016)**: the DCR was held to violate national treatment under GATT Article III:4 and the TRIMs Agreement, and India's "government procurement" defence was rejected. Hence the term's recurrence in the news → **(a)**.
questions.tagging_note: Straddles subjects: the term arises from the WTO solar dispute (ECO-13) but what is actually tested is knowledge of India's solar mission (ENV-16). Could defensibly be tagged ECO primary.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. The Nuclear Security Summits are periodically held under the aegis of the United Nations.
2. The International Panel on Fissile Materials is an organ of International Atomic Energy Agency.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Both are independent of UN/IAEA machinery.**

- **(1) Wrong.** The **Nuclear Security Summits (Washington 2010, Seoul 2012, The Hague 2014, Washington 2016) were a US-initiated process launched by President Obama** — a leaders-level political initiative, *not* held under the aegis of the United Nations. The series ended in 2016.
- **(2) Wrong.** The **International Panel on Fissile Materials (IPFM, 2006)** is an **independent group of arms-control and nuclear experts, based at Princeton University** — not an organ of the IAEA. It publishes the *Global Fissile Material Report*.

Neither → **(d)**.
questions.tagging_note: Nuclear Security Summits and the International Panel on Fissile Materials are non-treaty bodies; CAI-07 global governance is the nearest fit. Nuclear disarmament architecture (NPT/IAEA/NSG) is not an explicit topic in the tree.

questions.stem: Who among the following can join the National Pension System (NPS) ?
options: Persons of age from 21 to 55 only
All State Government employees joining the services after the date of notification by the respective State Governments
All Central Government employees including those of Armed Forces joining the services on or after 1st April, 2004
questions.explanation_md:
**The exclusion to remember: the Armed Forces are NOT in NPS.**

- **(a) Wrong.** **NRIs can also open an NPS account**, so "resident Indian citizens only" fails.
- **(b) Wrong.** The entry age is **18–60** (later extended to 65/70), not 21–55.
- **(c) Correct.** NPS applies to State Government employees who join **after the date each State notifies its adoption** of the scheme — different States switched over on different dates.
- **(d) Wrong.** NPS is mandatory for Central Government employees joining on or after **1 April 2004 — but the Armed Forces are expressly excluded.** The word "including Armed Forces" makes it false.

Answer **(c)**.
questions.tagging_note: Gap: nothing in the vocabulary covers pensions, PFRDA or social security products. ECO-06 (financial inclusion) and CAI-10 (schemes tracker) are both approximations, neither genuinely covers NPS eligibility rules.
questions.transcription_note: In option (d), '1st' is printed with a superscript 'st'.

questions.stem:
With reference to river Teesta, consider the following statements :
1. The source of river Teesta is the same as that of Brahmaputra but it flows through Sikkim.
2. River Rangeet originates in Sikkim and it is a tributary of river Teesta.
3. River Teesta flows into Bay of Bengal on the border of India and Bangladesh.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Only the Rangeet statement survives.**

- **(1) Wrong.** The **Brahmaputra rises from the Chemayungdung glacier near Mansarovar in Tibet**; the **Teesta rises from Tso Lhamo lake / Zemu glacier in North Sikkim**. Completely different sources.
- **(2) Correct.** The **Rangeet (Rangit)** rises from the Rathong glacier in West Sikkim and is the **largest tributary of the Teesta**, joining it near Teesta Bazaar/Melli on the Sikkim–West Bengal boundary.
- **(3) Wrong.** The Teesta enters Bangladesh at Kaliganj and **merges with the Brahmaputra (Jamuna) at Chilmari** — it never reaches the Bay of Bengal itself, and certainly not on the India–Bangladesh border.

Only 2 → **(b)**.
questions.tagging_note: Core drainage question (GEO-13); the Sikkim/Bangladesh course element is also atlas map work (GEO-24).

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. In tropical regions, Zika virus disease is transmitted by the same mosquito that transmits dengue.
2. Sexual transmission of Zika virus disease is possible.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Both statements are correct.**

1. **Correct.** Zika is spread by *Aedes aegypti* (and *Ae. albopictus*) — **the same mosquito that transmits dengue, chikungunya and yellow fever**. Day-biting, urban, breeds in clean stored water. This shared vector is why dengue-endemic India is a Zika-risk zone.
2. **Correct.** Zika is the **only major arbovirus with documented sexual transmission** — it persists in semen far longer than in blood, so WHO advises safe sex/abstinence for returning travellers. It also transmits vertically (mother to foetus → microcephaly) and via blood transfusion.

Answer: **(c) Both 1 and 2**

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. The Standard Mark of Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) is mandatory for automotive tyres and tubes.
2. AGMARK is a quality Certification Mark issued by the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Only statement 1 is correct.**

1. **Correct.** BIS certification is voluntary in general, but **mandatory for a notified list of products affecting health and safety** — including automotive tyres and tubes, cement, LPG cylinders, packaged drinking water, milk powder, helmets, electrical appliances.
2. **Wrong.** **AGMARK is issued by the Directorate of Marketing and Inspection (DMI), Ministry of Agriculture, Government of India**, under the Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937 — not by the FAO. It grades agricultural produce (ghee, honey, spices, pulses, vegetable oils).

Quick separation to hold: **BIS = industrial/manufactured goods; AGMARK = agricultural produce; FSSAI = food safety.**

Answer: **(a) 1 only**
questions.tagging_note: Gap in the vocabulary: no topic covers quality-certification marks and standards bodies (BIS, AGMARK, ISI, FSSAI). The question splits cleanly in two — statement 1 is industrial standards (nearest home ECO-15) and statement 2 is agricultural marketing certification (ECO-14). Neither topic names BIS or AGMARK; both are approximations.

questions.stem:
What is/are the advantage/advantages of implementing the 'National Agriculture Market' scheme ?
1. It is a pan-India electronic trading portal for agricultural commodities.
2. It provides the farmers access to nationwide market, with prices commensurate with the quality of their produce.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**Both statements are correct.** e-NAM (National Agriculture Market) was launched **14 April 2016**, run by the **Small Farmers' Agribusiness Consortium (SFAC)** under the Ministry of Agriculture.

1. **Correct.** It is a **pan-India electronic trading portal that networks existing APMC mandis** into one unified national market — not a parallel physical market.
2. **Correct.** Its core promise is that **assaying/quality grading at the mandi lets distant buyers bid**, so the farmer gets a price matched to the quality of the lot rather than to the handful of local traders present.

Answer: **(c) Both 1 and 2**
questions.tagging_note: e-NAM sits squarely in ECO-14 (APMC/agri-marketing reform); CAI-10 added because it is also a named government scheme tracked there.

questions.stem:
With reference to the 'National Intellectual Property Rights Policy', consider the following statements :
1. It reiterates India's commitment to the Doha Development Agenda and the TRIPS Agreement.
2. Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion is the nodal agency for regulating intellectual property rights in India.
Which of the above statements is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Both statements are correct.** National IPR Policy adopted **12 May 2016**; slogan *"Creative India; Innovative India"*; seven objectives.

1. **Correct.** The policy text **explicitly reaffirms India's commitment to the Doha Declaration on TRIPS and Public Health** and states that India's IPR regime is TRIPS-compliant — while retaining flexibilities like compulsory licensing and Section 3(d).
2. **Correct.** **DIPP (now DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry, is the nodal agency** for IPRs. In 2016 **copyright was shifted from the HRD Ministry to DIPP**, and the semiconductor layout-design law too, bringing all IPRs under one department; **CIPAM** was created under DIPP to implement the policy.

Answer: **(c) Both 1 and 2**
questions.tagging_note: Straddles economy and S&T: ECO-15 explicitly lists IPR and is the nodal-agency (DIPP/DPIIT) home; ECO-13 covers the WTO/TRIPS and Doha limb; SNT-14 covers IPR from the S&T-policy side.

questions.stem:
According to the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, which of the following animals cannot be hunted by any person except under some provisions provided by law ?
1. Gharial
2. Indian wild ass
3. Wild buffalo
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**All three are Schedule I animals** under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 — the highest protection, hunting barred except by permission of the Chief Wildlife Warden in narrow situations (man-eater, terminally ill/disabled animal, or for education/science).

1. **Gharial** — Schedule I. Critically Endangered; Chambal sanctuary.
2. **Indian wild ass (*Ghudkhur*)** — Schedule I. Little Rann of Kutch.
3. **Wild buffalo** — Schedule I. Endangered; Kaziranga, Manas, Indravati, Udanti.

The trap is assuming the wild ass or wild buffalo sits lower because it "looks like" livestock. **All three are Schedule I, so nothing is excluded.**

Answer: **(d) 1, 2 and 3**
questions.tagging_note: Matches the precedent tagging of the 2024 Q20 Wild Life (Protection) Act schedule question (ENV-09 primary, ENV-07 for the species knowledge).
questions.transcription_note: 'cannot' is printed in bold italics in the original; kept as plain text here. The stem also carries 'except under some provisions provided by law'.

questions.stem:
Which of the following statements is/are true of the Fundamental Duties of an Indian citizen ?
1. A legislative process has been provided to enforce these duties.
2. They are correlative to legal duties.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**Neither statement is correct.** Fundamental Duties: **Part IVA, Article 51A**, added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)** on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice; the 11th duty (education for 6–14 yrs) came via the **86th Amendment, 2002**.

1. **Wrong.** **The Constitution provides no mechanism or legislative process for enforcing the duties — they are non-justiciable and carry no legal sanction.** Swaran Singh Committee *did* recommend penalties for non-compliance, but the government **rejected** that recommendation. Parliament is free to legislate on a duty (e.g. Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act), but no enforcement process is *provided* by Part IVA itself.
2. **Wrong.** The Fundamental Duties are **moral and civic duties** (cherishing the ideals of the freedom struggle is moral; respecting the flag and anthem is civic). They are not legal duties, so they are not correlative to legal duties.

Answer: **(d) Neither 1 nor 2**

questions.stem:
Consider the following pairs :
1. Radhakanta Deb — First President of the British Indian Association
2. Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty — Founder of the Madras Mahajana Sabha
3. Surendranath Banerjee — Founder of the Indian Association
Which of the above pairs is/are correctly matched ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Pairs 1 and 3 are correct.**

1. **Correct.** **British Indian Association, Calcutta, 1851** (merger of Landholders' Society + Bengal British India Society). **Radhakanta Deb was its first President**, Debendranath Tagore its Secretary — a landlord-dominated body.
2. **Wrong.** **Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty founded the Madras Native Association (1852)** and the newspaper *The Crescent*. **The Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884) was founded by M. Viraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer and P. Anandacharlu.**
3. **Correct.** **Indian Association, 1876, Calcutta — Surendranath Banerjee with Anandamohan Bose**, the most important pre-Congress nationalist body; it led the Ilbert Bill and civil-service age-limit agitations.

Answer: **(b) 1 and 3 only**
questions.tagging_note: All three pairs are pre-Congress and early-Congress political associations (British Indian Association, Madras Mahajana Sabha, Indian Association), which HIS-06 covers directly. Format is stmt_1_2_3, not pairs — 'pairs' is reserved in question-formats.json for the 'how many pairs are correct' counting variant.

questions.stem: Which one of the following objectives is **not** embodied in the Preamble to the Constitution of India ?
questions.explanation_md:
The Preamble grants **"LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship"** — five items, and **"economic liberty" is not among them**.

Memory hook for the Preamble's four ideals:
- **JUSTICE** — social, economic and political *(economic appears here, under justice — that is the bait in this question)*
- **LIBERTY** — thought, expression, belief, faith, worship
- **EQUALITY** — of status and of opportunity
- **FRATERNITY** — assuring dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the Nation

Answer: **(b) Economic liberty**

questions.stem:
With reference to 'Quality Council of India (QCI)', consider the following statements :
1. QCI was set up jointly by the Government of India and the Indian Industry.
2. Chairman of QCI is appointed by the Prime Minister on the recommendations of the industry to the Government.
Which of the above statements is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Both statements are correct.** QCI was set up in **1997 as a non-profit autonomous society**, registered under the Societies Registration Act.

1. **Correct.** It was established **jointly by the Government of India (DIPP, Ministry of Commerce and Industry as nodal ministry) and the three industry bodies — ASSOCHAM, CII and FICCI**, on a public–private partnership basis.
2. **Correct.** **The Chairman of QCI is appointed by the Prime Minister on the recommendation of the industry to the government** — an unusual arrangement worth memorising, since it is the fact this question turns on. QCI operates the accreditation boards (NABL, NABH, NABCB, NABET) and ran the *Swachh Survekshan* surveys.

Answer: **(c) Both 1 and 2**
questions.tagging_note: Real gap: no topic covers standards/accreditation institutions (QCI, NABL, NABH, BIS). ECO-15 is the nearest home following the 2026 Q29 certification precedent; POL-25 added because QCI is a non-constitutional, non-statutory body and statement 2 tests the appointment mechanism, which is governance-flavoured. Neither topic names QCI.

questions.stem:
What is the purpose of setting up of Small Finance Banks (SFBs) in India ?
1. To supply credit to small business units
2. To supply credit to small and marginal farmers
3. To encourage young entrepreneurs to set up business particularly in rural areas.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**Statements 1 and 2 only.** RBI's stated objective for Small Finance Banks (guidelines 2014; first licences 2015–16, e.g. Ujjivan, Equitas, AU) is **furthering financial inclusion** by two means: savings vehicles for the unserved/underserved, and **supply of credit to small business units; small and marginal farmers; micro and small industries; and other unorganised-sector entities**, through high-technology, low-cost operations.

1. **Correct** — named verbatim in the objective.
2. **Correct** — named verbatim in the objective.
3. **Wrong.** **"Encouraging young entrepreneurs" is nowhere in the SFB mandate** — that is the language of MUDRA/Stand-Up India/Start-up India. SFBs are defined by *whom they lend to* (small borrowers), not by the borrower's age.

Key norms to carry: minimum paid-up capital **Rs 200 crore**, **75% of ANBC to priority sector**, **50% of the loan book in loans up to Rs 25 lakh**.

Answer: **(a) 1 and 2 only**
questions.tagging_note: ECO-04 names SFBs explicitly; ECO-06 covers the financial-inclusion purpose the three statements describe.

questions.stem:
With reference to 'Asia Pacific Ministerial Conference on Housing and Urban Development (APMCHUD)', consider the following statements :
1. The first APMCHUD was held in India in 2006 on the theme 'Emerging Urban Forms — Policy Responses and Governance Structure'.
2. India hosts all the Annual Ministerial Conferences in partnership with ADB, APEC and ASEAN.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Answer: (d) Neither 1 nor 2**

### Statement 1 — false, and it is false only in its last clause

Everything in statement 1 that the eye checks first is true. The **first APMCHUD really was held in India, in New Delhi, in December 2006**. So the statement reads as correct right up to the theme — and the theme is where UPSC put the error.

- **1st APMCHUD, New Delhi, 13–16 December 2006** — theme: *"A Vision for Sustainable Urbanisation in the Asia-Pacific by 2020"*. Its outcome document was the (first) New Delhi Declaration.
- **6th APMCHUD, New Delhi, 14–16 December 2016** — theme: *"Emerging Urban Forms — Policy Responses and Governance Structure"* (in the context of the New Urban Agenda). 68 countries attended; it produced the 2016 Delhi Declaration.

The statement is a **date–theme splice**: two genuine facts about two genuine India-hosted conferences, welded into one sentence. India + first + 2006 belongs to one conference; the quoted theme belongs to a different one, ten years later.

The 2016 conference is the whole reason this question appeared in the 2017 paper. It was a December 2016 news item, six months before the exam. UPSC was not asking *"did India host the first APMCHUD?"* — it was asking *"did you actually read the news item, or only register that India hosted something?"* A candidate who read it knows the Emerging Urban Forms theme is the **sixth** conference's, and that gives the whole statement away.

### Why (a) "1 only" fails

(a) is the natural answer for a solver who verifies the checkable, high-salience facts — country, ordinal, year — finds all three correct, and treats the long quoted theme as decoration. It is not decoration. A quoted theme inside a statement is a claim like any other, and here it is the **only** false part. Statement 1 asserts a conjunction: first + India + 2006 + *that theme*. Three true conjuncts and one false one make the statement false. Getting India and 2006 right is exactly the bait — the statement is engineered so the recallable half is correct.

### Statement 2 — false three separate times over

Any one of these sinks it:

1. **"India hosts all"** — the quantifier. Hosting rotates: 2nd Tehran (2008), 3rd Solo, Indonesia (2010), 4th Amman, Jordan (2012), 5th Seoul, Republic of Korea (2014), 6th New Delhi (2016). India has hosted two of six.
2. **"Annual"** — APMCHUD is **biennial**, held every two years, as the 2006–2008–2010–2012–2014–2016 sequence shows on its face.
3. **"in partnership with ADB, APEC and ASEAN"** — wrong body entirely. APMCHUD is an inter-governmental mechanism established **under the aegis and support of UN-Habitat**. ADB, APEC and ASEAN are plausible-sounding Asia-Pacific acronyms substituted for the real one.

### The takeaway

Two different failure modes in one question. Statement 2 fails on a **quantifier and a substituted institution** — the standard UPSC tells. Statement 1 fails on a **spliced attribute**: a real theme attached to the wrong edition of a real conference. When a statement quotes a specific named theme, summit number, or declaration, that quoted string is the thing being tested, not the country and year around it.
questions.tagging_note: APMCHUD is an obscure Asia-Pacific ministerial forum on housing/urban development. No topic in the vocabulary names it or covers 'international conferences/forums on urban development'; CAI-05 (regional groupings) is the nearest home because statement 2 turns on ADB/APEC/ASEAN, with CAI-04 as fallback. Genuinely straddles urbanisation (GEO-22) but the testable content is the grouping, not urban geography.
questions.review_flag: Official key says d, worked solution said a (medium confidence).

questions.stem: Democracy's superior virtue lies in the fact that it calls into activity
options: the intelligence and character of ordinary men and women.
the methods for strengthening executive leadership.
a superior individual with dynamism and vision.
a band of dedicated party workers.
questions.explanation_md:
A value-judgement question — UPSC always rewards the **participatory, citizen-centred** option.

The phrasing echoes **J.S. Mill and Lord Bryce: democracy's unique merit is that participation itself educates and elevates the ordinary citizen**, developing intelligence and character in people an autocracy would leave passive.

- (b) strong executive — an argument for presidential/authoritarian rule, not democracy's virtue.
- (c) a superior individual with vision — Carlyle's 'great man' theory, i.e. the *opposite* of democracy.
- (d) dedicated party workers — describes a cadre party, not a democracy.

→ **(a)**
questions.tagging_note: Pure political-theory question on the virtue of democracy — no article, body or judgment involved. The vocabulary has no 'political theory / concepts of democracy, liberty, equality' topic (SOC-25 covers democracy only inside the Sociology optional). POL-03 'Salient Features of the Constitution' (democratic republic) is the least-bad fit. This is a real gap in the syllabus tree: UPSC asks 2-4 such conceptual polity questions a year.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a most likely consequence of implementing the 'Unified Payments Interface (UPI)' ?
options: Mobile wallets will not be necessary for online payments.
Digital currency will totally replace the physical currency in about two decades.
Direct transfer of subsidies to poor people will become very effective.
questions.explanation_md:
UPI (launched by **NPCI, April 2016**) lets you push money **bank account to bank account instantly using only a Virtual Payment Address**, on a 24x7 basis, from any UPI app.

**Because funds move straight from the bank account, there is no need to pre-load cash into a mobile wallet (PPI) at all** — that is the direct, immediate consequence. UPI made wallets' core function redundant.

- (b) 'digital totally replaces physical currency in two decades' — speculative, no basis.
- (c) FDI inflows — unrelated to a retail payments rail.
- (d) DBT subsidy transfer already runs on **Aadhaar Payment Bridge / NACH**, a government-to-citizen push; UPI is a person-to-person/merchant pull system and is not the DBT channel.

→ **(a)**

questions.stem: The terms 'Event Horizon', 'Singularity', 'String Theory' and 'Standard Model' are sometimes seen in the news in the context of
options: Observation and understanding of the Universe
Study of the solar and the lunar eclipses
Placing satellites in the orbit of the Earth
Origin and evolution of living organisms on the Earth
questions.explanation_md:
All four terms belong to **cosmology and fundamental physics**:

- **Event horizon** — the boundary of a black hole beyond which nothing, not even light, escapes.
- **Singularity** — the infinite-density point at a black hole's centre and at the Big Bang.
- **String theory** — candidate 'theory of everything' treating particles as vibrating strings, an attempt to unify gravity with quantum mechanics.
- **Standard Model** — the framework of 17 fundamental particles (quarks, leptons, force carriers, Higgs).

**Together they are the vocabulary of how the Universe began, is structured and is observed** — nothing to do with eclipses, satellite launches or biological evolution. → **(a)**
questions.tagging_note: Straddles SNT (astronomy/physics vocabulary — black holes, Standard Model) and GEO-01 (universe). Primary kept in SNT because the terms are physics-of-the-universe, not positional astronomy.

questions.stem:
With reference to agriculture in India, how can the technique of 'genome sequencing', often seen in the news, be used in the immediate future ?
1. Genome sequencing can be used to identify genetic markers for disease resistance and drought tolerance in various crop plants.
2. This technique helps in reducing the time required to develop new varieties of crop plants.
3. It can be used to decipher the host-pathogen relationships in crops.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
Genome sequencing reads the full DNA of a crop or its pathogen. All three uses are real and already operational.

- **St. 1 — correct.** Sequencing locates **QTLs and SNP markers** linked to disease resistance and drought tolerance (e.g. the *Sub1A* submergence gene in rice, drought QTLs in chickpea and pigeonpea sequenced by ICRISAT).
- **St. 2 — correct.** It enables **marker-assisted selection, which replaces years of field phenotyping and cuts variety-development time** from ~10-12 years to a few breeding cycles.
- **St. 3 — correct.** Sequencing *both* host and pathogen (e.g. wheat vs *Puccinia* rust, rice vs *Magnaporthe* blast) reveals the R-gene/avirulence-gene interaction — exactly how host-pathogen relationships are deciphered.

No statement is futuristic or false. → **(d)**
questions.tagging_note: Biotechnology technique applied to crops; GEO-17 (India agriculture) is a secondary, weaker link.

questions.stem: The main advantage of the parliamentary form of government is that
options: the executive and legislature work independently.
it provides continuity of policy and is more efficient.
the executive remains responsible to the legislature.
the head of the government cannot be changed without election.
questions.explanation_md:
**The defining feature — and chief advantage — of the parliamentary system is collective responsibility: the Council of Ministers is answerable to the Lok Sabha and stays in office only while it holds its confidence** (Art. 75(3)). That daily accountability is what a presidential system lacks.

- (a) independent executive and legislature — that is the **presidential** system's separation of powers, not parliamentary (where the executive sits *in* the legislature).
- (b) continuity and efficiency — actually a **demerit** of parliamentary government; coalitions and no-confidence motions make it *less* stable than a fixed-term presidency.
- (d) head of government cannot be changed without election — false; a PM can be removed any day by a no-confidence vote or by losing party support.

→ **(c)**

questions.stem: In the context of India, which one of the following is the correct relationship between Rights and Duties ?
options: Rights are personal and hence independent of society and Duties.
Rights, not Duties, are important for the advancement of the personality of the citizen.
Duties, not Rights, are important for the stability of the State.
questions.explanation_md:
**Rights and duties are correlative — every right of one person implies a corresponding duty on others (and on oneself) to respect it.** My right to free speech imposes a duty on you not to silence me, and a duty on me not to defame you. Rights exist only within society; they are claims recognised by the community.

The Constitution mirrors this: **Part III Fundamental Rights (Arts. 12-35) are paired with Part IVA Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A)**, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976 on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice.

- (b) is wrong because rights are *social* claims, meaningless for a person alone.
- (c) and (d) each elevate one at the expense of the other — the balanced, correlative view is the constitutional position.

→ **(a)**
questions.tagging_note: Conceptual question on rights being correlative with duties rather than on any specific article. POL-12 (Fundamental Duties) is the closest topic; POL-07 added as the general Fundamental Rights entry point. Like Q42, it exposes the absence of a political-theory topic.

questions.stem: The mind of the makers of the Constitution of India is reflected in which of the following ?
options: The Directive Principles of State Policy
questions.explanation_md:
**The Preamble is the 'identity card of the Constitution' (N.A. Palkhivala) and, in the words of the Supreme Court, contains the ideals and aspirations of the Constituent Assembly — the mind of the makers.**

It grew directly out of Nehru's **Objectives Resolution (13 Dec 1946)**, adopted 22 Jan 1947, so it literally records what the framers set out to achieve: Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic; Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.

- Fundamental Rights and DPSPs are the *means and goals* enacted; Fundamental Duties came only in **1976 (42nd Amendment)** — long after the makers finished, so they cannot reflect their mind at all.
- Berubari Union (1960) called the Preamble the 'key to open the mind of the makers'; Kesavananda (1973) held it part of the Constitution.

→ **(a)**

questions.stem: If you travel by road from Kohima to Kottayam, what is the minimum number of States within India through which you can travel, including the origin and the destination ?
questions.explanation_md:
Kohima is in **Nagaland**, Kottayam in **Kerala**. Trace the shortest chain of contiguous states:

**Nagaland → Assam → West Bengal → Odisha → Andhra Pradesh → Tamil Nadu → Kerala = 7 states.**

Key links to remember:
- Nagaland's only useful western neighbour is Assam.
- **Assam touches West Bengal at the narrow Siliguri 'chicken neck' corridor** — this is the one link candidates miss, and it is what keeps the count at 7 rather than higher.
- Odisha does not touch any state bordering Kerala, and **Andhra Pradesh does not border Kerala**, so one more southern state is unavoidable: either Tamil Nadu or Karnataka (both give 7).

Six is impossible; you cannot bridge Odisha to Kerala in a single hop. → **(b) 7**
questions.tagging_note: Pure map/atlas question — counting states on a Kohima-to-Kottayam road route. GEO-24 (map work) is the correct home; GEO-12 secondary.

questions.stem:
The Parliament of India exercises control over the functions of the Council of Ministers through
1. Adjournment motion
2. Question hour
3. Supplementary questions
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**All three are recognised parliamentary devices for enforcing ministerial responsibility under Art. 75(3).**

- **St. 1 — correct.** The **adjournment motion** sets aside normal business to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance; it carries an **element of censure** and is available only in the **Lok Sabha** (needs 50 members' support). Clearly a control device.
- **St. 2 — correct.** **Question Hour** (first hour, 11 am-12 noon) — starred, unstarred and short-notice questions compel ministers to answer for their departments.
- **St. 3 — correct.** **Supplementary questions** follow an oral (starred) answer; the ability to probe unrehearsed is precisely where a minister is held to account.

Nothing here is a budget or legislative device wrongly slipped in, so nothing is excludable. → **(d)**
questions.tagging_note: Parliamentary devices (adjournment motion, question hour, supplementary questions) sit in POL-18; POL-17 added because the object of control is the Council of Ministers.

questions.stem: Which one of the following was a very important seaport in the Kakatiya kingdom ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Motupalli** (Prakasam district, Andhra Pradesh) was the great seaport of the Kakatiyas.

- **Ganapatideva issued the *Motupalli Abhaya Shasanam* (c. 1244–45), a bilingual (Sanskrit–Telugu) charter guaranteeing safety of foreign merchants' ships and goods** — a fixed customs duty in place of arbitrary seizure of wrecked cargo. This inscription is the deciding fact.
- Marco Polo visited the port during Rudramadevi's reign and praised its fine muslin.
- Machilipatnam rose later under the Qutb Shahis/Europeans; Kakinada and Nellore are not associated with Kakatiya maritime trade.
questions.tagging_note: The Kakatiyas (Warangal, 12th–14th c.) are not named anywhere in the vocabulary. ANM-09 'Cholas and the South Indian dynasties' is the nearest genuine home; ANM-12 (regional kingdoms of the Deccan) is the alternative. A dedicated Deccan/Kakatiya-Yadava slot is missing from the tree.

questions.stem:
With reference to 'Global Climate Change Alliance', which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. It is an initiative of the European Union.
2. It provides technical and financial support to targeted developing countries to integrate climate change into their development policies and budgets.
3. It is coordinated by World Resources Institute (WRI) and World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD).
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**GCCA is an EU initiative (launched 2007 by the European Commission), later GCCA+.**

1. **Correct** — EU initiative, targeting LDCs and Small Island Developing States.
2. **Correct** — provides technical assistance and finance to mainstream climate change into national development plans and budgets (adaptation, DRR, REDD, CDM).
3. **Wrong** — WRI + WBCSD jointly coordinate the **Greenhouse Gas Protocol**, not the GCCA. GCCA is run by the European Commission (DG DEVCO/INTPA).

So 1 and 2 only.

questions.stem:
With reference to the religious history of India, consider the following statements :
1. Sautrantika and Sammitiya were the sects of Jainism.
2. Sarvastivadin held that the constituents of phenomena were not wholly momentary, but existed forever in a latent form.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
1. **Wrong** — **Sautrantika and Sammitiya are Buddhist sects, not Jain.** Sautrantika accepted only the Sutta Pitaka as authoritative (hence the name); Sammitiya was a Hinayana offshoot of the Vatsiputriyas (pudgalavadins). Jain sects are Digambara/Svetambara, Yapaniya, Sthanakvasi, Terapanthi.
2. **Correct** — the **Sarvastivadins ('all exists') held that dharmas exist in past, present and future** — phenomena are not wholly momentary but persist in a latent state. This is the doctrine that gives the school its name.

Only 2.
questions.tagging_note: Sautrantika, Sammitiya and Sarvastivada are Buddhist schools — squarely the heterodox-sects topic; the Jainism mis-attribution is the trap.

questions.stem:
Mediterranean Sea is a border of which of the following countries ?
1. Jordan
2. Iraq
3. Lebanon
4. Syria
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**The Mediterranean's eastern (Levantine) coast, north to south: Turkey – Syria – Lebanon – Israel – Gaza – Egypt.**

1. Jordan — **no**. Landlocked except for a tiny outlet at Aqaba on the **Red Sea** (Gulf of Aqaba).
2. Iraq — **no**. Its only coast is a short stretch on the **Persian Gulf**.
3. Lebanon — **yes**, entire western coast (Beirut, Tripoli).
4. Syria — **yes** (Latakia, Tartus — Russia's naval facility).

So 3 and 4 only.
questions.tagging_note: Pure world-atlas recall (West Asian coastlines). Only GEO-24 map work covers it; there is no world political/regional geography topic in the tree. Format is a numbered option list rather than statements, mapped to stmt_1_2_3 as the closest available shape.

questions.stem:
With reference to 'National Investment and Infrastructure Fund', which of the following statements is/are correct ?
1. It is an organ of NITI Aayog.
2. It has a corpus of ₹ 4,00,000 crore at present.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**NIIF (2015) is a fund set up by the Government of India under the Ministry of Finance, registered with SEBI as an Alternative Investment Fund — nothing to do with NITI Aayog, and its corpus is ₹40,000 crore, not ₹4,00,000 crore.**

1. **Wrong** — it is not an organ of NITI Aayog. NIIF Ltd. is the investment manager; Govt. holds 49%, the rest from domestic and foreign investors (ADIA, Temasek, AIIB etc.).
2. **Wrong** — planned corpus ₹40,000 crore, with the Centre contributing 49% (~₹20,000 crore).

Neither 1 nor 2.
questions.tagging_note: NIIF is not named in the vocabulary. It sits between ECO-16 (infrastructure financing, PPP) and ECO-08 (it is a SEBI-registered AIF). Statement 1 also brushes NITI Aayog (POL-25), but that is the distractor, not what is tested.

questions.stem: The Global Infrastructure Facility is a/an
options: ASEAN initiative to upgrade infrastructure in Asia and financed by credit from the Asian Development Bank.

World Bank collaboration that facilitates the preparation and structuring of complex infrastructure Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) to enable mobilization of private sector and institutional investor capital.
Collaboration among the major banks of the world working with the OECD and focused on expanding the set of infrastructure projects that have the potential to mobilize private investment.
UNCTAD funded initiative that seeks to finance and facilitate infrastructure development in the world.
questions.explanation_md:
**The Global Infrastructure Facility (GIF) is a World Bank Group–managed global platform (launched 2014) that helps governments prepare and structure complex infrastructure PPPs so that private and institutional capital can be mobilised.**

- It is a partnership of governments, MDBs, private financiers and investors, housed at the World Bank — not ASEAN/ADB, not OECD-led, not UNCTAD.
- Do not confuse with the **Global Infrastructure Hub**, a G20 initiative, or with **Blue Dot Network**.
questions.tagging_note: Straddles ECO-13 (World Bank family of institutions) and ECO-16 (infrastructure PPP mobilisation); the answer hinges on identifying the World Bank as sponsor, so ECO-13 leads.

questions.stem: For election to the Lok Sabha, a nomination paper can be filed by
options: a resident of the constituency from which the election is to be contested.
any citizen of India whose name appears in the electoral roll of a constituency.
questions.explanation_md:
**RPA 1951, s.4: to contest a Lok Sabha seat you must be an elector (name on the electoral roll) in *any* parliamentary constituency in India — not necessarily the one being contested.**

- So mere citizenship is not enough (option d): a citizen disqualified from or not enrolled in any roll cannot stand.
- Residence in that particular constituency is **not** required for Lok Sabha (option b is wrong).
- Note the contrast: for **Rajya Sabha**, since the 2003 amendment, the candidate must be an elector in any parliamentary constituency in India too (domicile requirement removed); for **Assembly** seats, one must be an elector in a constituency in that State.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. In India, the Himalayas are spread over five States only.
2. Western Ghats are spread over five States only.
3. Pulicat Lake is spread over two States only.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
1. **Wrong** — the Indian Himalaya runs through far more than five States: J&K, Ladakh, Himachal, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, West Bengal, Arunachal, plus the Purvanchal/eastern hill States (Assam hills, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Meghalaya per the standard extended count). At least 11–12 States/UTs.
2. **Wrong** — Western Ghats run through **six** States: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu. (Counting from the Tapi/Satpura edge in Gujarat is what makes it six, not five — this is the trap.)
3. **Correct** — **Pulicat Lake, India's second-largest brackish lagoon, lies across Andhra Pradesh (~84%) and Tamil Nadu (~16%) only**, separated from the Bay of Bengal by Sriharikota island.

So 3 only.

questions.stem: Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD) is a standard criterion for
options: Computing oxygen levels in forest ecosystems
Assessing oxygen levels in high altitude regions
questions.explanation_md:
**BOD is the amount of dissolved oxygen consumed by aerobic microbes in breaking down organic matter in a water sample (standard test: 5 days at 20°C, mg/L).**

- **High BOD = high organic/sewage load = polluted water**, because microbes strip oxygen from the water, killing fish. So it is a measure of organic pollution in **aquatic ecosystems**.
- Clean river water: BOD < 3 mg/L; raw sewage: hundreds of mg/L. CPCB's bathing-water criterion is BOD ≤ 3 mg/L.
- It has nothing to do with blood, forests or altitude.

questions.stem:
With reference to the role of UN-Habitat in the United Nations programme working towards a better urban future, which of the statements is/are correct ?
1. UN-Habitat has been mandated by the United Nations General Assembly to promote socially and environmentally sustainable towns and cities to provide adequate shelter for all.
2. Its partners are either governments or local urban authorities only.
3. UN-Habitat contributes to the overall objective of the United Nations system to reduce poverty and to promote access to safe drinking water and basic sanitation.
Select the correct answer using the code given below ;
questions.explanation_md:
**UN-Habitat (Nairobi, est. 1978; upgraded to a full UN programme by UNGA in 2002) — 'socially and environmentally sustainable towns and cities with adequate shelter for all' is literally its mandate.**

1. **Correct** — that is the UNGA-mandated mission statement.
2. **Wrong** — the giveaway word is **'only'**. UN-Habitat works with NGOs, civil society, research and academic bodies, the private sector, professional associations and other UN agencies, not just governments and local authorities.
3. **Correct** — it contributes to the UN system goals of poverty reduction and access to safe water and basic sanitation (the old MDG 7 Target 10/11 work, slum upgrading).

So 1 and 3 only. In statement-based questions, an absolute qualifier like 'only' on a partnership list is almost always the wrong statement.
questions.tagging_note: UN-Habitat is a UN programme, so CAI-04 (UN and multilateral bodies) fits the mandate/partners statements; the subject matter (sustainable towns, shelter, sanitation) overlaps GEO-22 settlements and urbanisation. No topic names UN specialised agencies individually.

questions.stem:
With reference to 'National Skills Qualification Framework (NSQF)', which of the statements given below is/are correct ?
1. Under NSQF, a learner can acquire the certification for competency only through formal learning.
2. An outcome expected from the implementation of NSQF is the mobility between vocational and general education.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**NSQF explicitly recognises prior learning — competency acquired informally or non-formally can be certified through RPL.** So statement 1 ("only through formal learning") is wrong.

- **St. 1 — wrong.** NSQF is *outcome-based*: it certifies what a learner can do, however they learnt it. Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) exists precisely for the informally skilled worker.
