- **St. 2 — correct.** Stated objectives include multiple entry/exit points and **horizontal and vertical mobility between vocational and general education**, plus alignment with international frameworks.

NSQF: notified 2013, organises qualifications in **10 levels** by knowledge, skill and aptitude; anchored under the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship.
questions.tagging_note: Skill development / vocational-education frameworks (NSQF, NSDC, PMKVY) have no dedicated topic in the vocabulary — the nearest homes are ECO-17 (unemployment and employability schemes) and ECO-18 (education indicators), with CAI-10 as the schemes tracker. This is a genuine gap in the syllabus tree.

questions.stem: In the context of Indian history, the principle of 'Dyarchy (diarchy)' refers to
options: Division of the central legislature into two houses.
Introduction of double government i.e., Central and State governments.
Having two sets of rulers; one in London and another in Delhi.
Division of the subjects delegated to the provinces into two categories.
questions.explanation_md:
**Dyarchy = the Government of India Act 1919 (Montagu–Chelmsford) splitting provincial subjects into "Transferred" and "Reserved".**

- **Transferred** subjects (education, local self-government, health, agriculture, public works) — administered by the Governor with ministers responsible to the legislative council.
- **Reserved** subjects (police, land revenue, irrigation, justice, press) — administered by the Governor with his Executive Council, not answerable to the legislature.

Only **provincial** subjects were divided, so "double government i.e., Central and State" (option b) is wrong. Dyarchy in provinces was abolished by the **GoI Act 1935**, which introduced provincial autonomy and instead prescribed dyarchy **at the Centre** (never implemented).

questions.stem:
Consider the following in respect of 'National Career Service' :
1. National Career Service is an initiative of the Department of Personnel and Training, Government of India.
2. National Career Service has been launched in a Mission Mode to improve the employment opportunities to uneducated youth of the country.
Which of the above statements is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**National Career Service belongs to the Ministry of Labour and Employment, not DoPT.**

- **St. 1 — wrong.** Launched July 2015 by the **Ministry of Labour & Employment**; DoPT (Ministry of Personnel) deals with civil-service administration, not employment exchanges.
- **St. 2 — wrong.** It is a mission-mode project, but it serves **all job-seekers** — a portal linking jobseekers, employers, career counsellors, skill providers and modernised employment exchanges. It is not restricted to "uneducated youth".

Both halves fail, so **Neither 1 nor 2**.
questions.tagging_note: National Career Service is an employment-exchange scheme; tested as a scheme-facts question, so CAI-10 (schemes tracker) is a genuine second home.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best describes the term 'Scheme for Sustainable Structuring of Stressed Assets (S4A)', recently seen in the news ?
options: It is a procedure for considering ecological costs of developmental schemes formulated by the Government.
It is a scheme of RBI for reworking the financial structure of big corporate entities facing genuine difficulties.
It is a disinvestment plan of the Government regarding Central Public Sector Undertakings.
It is an important provision in 'The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code' recently implemented by the Government.
questions.explanation_md:
**S4A is an RBI scheme (June 2016) for restructuring the debt of large stressed corporate borrowers.**

Mechanics: for projects that have commenced commercial operations with aggregate exposure above **₹500 crore**, the outstanding debt is split into —
- **Part A** — the *sustainable* portion (at least 50%) that current cash flows can service, kept as debt;
- **Part B** — the *unsustainable* remainder, converted into equity / redeemable optionally-convertible preference shares.

No change in promoter ownership is required, and there is **no fresh moratorium or interest-rate concession** — that is what separates it from CDR/SDR. It is an RBI regulatory scheme, not a clause of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC) to Reduce Short Lived Climate Pollutants is a unique initiative of G20 group of countries.
2. The CCAC focuses on methane, black carbon and hydrofluorocarbons.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**CCAC was launched in 2012 by UNEP with six founding countries — it is not a G20 initiative.**

- **St. 1 — wrong.** Founders: Bangladesh, Canada, Ghana, Mexico, Sweden, USA + UNEP. It is a voluntary multi-stakeholder partnership (governments, IGOs, NGOs, private sector), hosted by UNEP in Paris. India is *not* a member.
- **St. 2 — correct.** It targets short-lived climate pollutants: **methane, black carbon and HFCs** (tropospheric ozone is also addressed, largely via its methane precursor).

SLCPs have short atmospheric lifetimes, so cutting them delivers near-term warming and air-quality benefits.

questions.stem:
With reference to 'Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)' sometimes mentioned in the news while forecasting Indian monsoon, which of the following statements is/are correct ?
1. IOD phenomenon is characterised by a difference in sea surface temperature between tropical Western Indian Ocean and tropical Eastern Pacific Ocean.
2. An IOD phenomenon can influence an El Nino's impact on the monsoon.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**IOD is measured entirely within the Indian Ocean — western Arabian Sea vs eastern Indian Ocean off Sumatra/Java. The Pacific does not enter the definition.**

- **St. 1 — wrong.** The stated "tropical Eastern **Pacific** Ocean" is the giveaway; the correct pole is the tropical **eastern Indian** Ocean.
- **St. 2 — correct.** A **positive IOD** (warm west, cool east) strengthens the monsoon and can offset or mask the drought-inducing effect of an El Niño — 1997 is the classic case: strong El Niño, yet a normal Indian monsoon because of a strong +IOD. A negative IOD compounds El Niño's damage.

IOD is also called the "Indian Niño".

questions.stem: If you want to see gharials in their natural habitat, which one of the following is the best place to visit ?
questions.explanation_md:
**The National Chambal Sanctuary holds the largest wild breeding population of gharial (*Gavialis gangeticus*).**

The gharial is a **freshwater, fish-eating, riverine** crocodilian — it needs clean sandbanks for basking and nesting, which the Chambal (spanning MP, Rajasthan, UP) provides. IUCN **Critically Endangered**; Schedule I.

Why the others fail:
- **Bhitarkanika** — brackish mangrove, famous for the **saltwater crocodile**.
- **Pulicat** — brackish coastal lagoon, flamingos.
- **Deepor Beel** — Assam Ramsar wetland, waterfowl and elephants, no gharial.

questions.stem:
Consider the following in respect of Indian Ocean Naval Symposium (IONS) :
1. Inaugural IONS was held in India in 2015 under the chairmanship of the Indian Navy.
2. IONS is a voluntary initiative that seeks to increase maritime co-operation among navies of the littoral states of the Indian Ocean Region.
Which of the above statements is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**The inaugural IONS was held at New Delhi in February 2008, not 2015.**

- **St. 1 — wrong on the date.** India did host it and the Indian Navy did chair the first two-year term (2008–10), but the year was **2008**. Chairmanship has since rotated (UAE, South Africa, Australia, Bangladesh, Iran, France, Thailand…).
- **St. 2 — correct.** IONS is a **voluntary** initiative to increase maritime cooperation among navies of Indian Ocean **littoral** states — a forum for dialogue on HADR, information sharing and interoperability. It has no treaty obligations.

Watch the date: UPSC's favourite trap in this question type.
questions.tagging_note: IONS is a maritime-security grouping of Indian Ocean littoral navies. It is not named in any topic; CAI-05 (regional groupings, incl. IORA) is the closest fit, CAI-04 covers the multilateral-grouping habit, and the naval angle brushes SNT-07. Maritime security as a theme is thinly covered in the vocabulary.

questions.stem: The painting of Bodhisattva Padmapani is one of the most famous and oft-illustrated paintings at
questions.explanation_md:
**Padmapani (and its companion Vajrapani) are painted on the walls flanking the shrine antechamber of Cave 1 at Ajanta** — Vakataka period, c. 5th century CE, Mahayana phase.

The bodhisattva holds a **blue lotus (padma)**, head gently inclined, eyes half-closed — the "compassionate gaze". Technique is **tempera on a mud-plaster ground**, not true fresco.

Distinguish: **Bagh** caves (MP) have related paintings; **Badami** Cave 3 has Chalukyan paintings; **Ellora** has some Kailasa ceiling painting — but Padmapani is the signature Ajanta image.

questions.stem:
Consider the following pairs :

| | *Traditions* | *Communities* |
|---|---|---|
| 1. | Chaliha Sahib Festival | Sindhis |
| 2. | Nanda Raj Jaat Yatra | Gonds |
| 3. | Wari-Warkari | Santhals |

Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Only pair 1 matches.**

1. **Chaliha Sahib — Sindhis. Correct.** A 40-day observance (*chaliha* = forty) honouring **Jhulelal / Varun Dev**, the Sindhi water deity; observed with fasting and abstinence, mainly around Ulhasnagar and other Sindhi settlements.
2. **Nanda Raj Jat Yatra — Gonds. Wrong.** It is the Himalayan pilgrimage of **Uttarakhand** (Garhwal–Kumaon), held roughly once every 12 years, honouring goddess Nanda Devi; a four-horned ram leads the procession to Homkund. Gonds are of central India.
3. **Wari–Warkari — Santhals. Wrong.** The **Varkari** tradition of **Maharashtra** — the annual *wari* (foot pilgrimage) carrying palkhis of Sant Dnyaneshwar and Tukaram to **Pandharpur** (Vitthal), on Ashadhi Ekadashi. Santhals are a tribe of Jharkhand/WB/Odisha.
questions.tagging_note: Format: pair-matching with 'which is/are correctly matched' rather than a 'how many' count — tagged pairs on content, not the count-phrasing rule. Content is community festivals and traditions (ART-09 fairs and festivals); Wari-Warkari is also a living Bhakti tradition, hence ANM-13.

questions.stem:
Which of the following practices can help in water conservation in agriculture ?
1. Reduced or zero tillage of the land
2. Applying gypsum before irrigating the field
3. Allowing crop residue to remain in the field
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**Statement 1 — correct.** Zero/reduced tillage leaves the soil undisturbed, so pore structure and capillary continuity survive, infiltration improves and evaporation from a churned-up surface is avoided. Core of conservation agriculture.

**Statement 2 — incorrect (the deciding statement).** Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) is a **soil amendment for sodic/alkali soils** — Ca²⁺ displaces exchangeable Na⁺, which is then leached out. Its purpose is reclamation of sodicity, and reclamation actually needs *extra* leaching water. It is not a water-conservation practice.

**Statement 3 — correct.** Crop residue left on the surface acts as mulch: cuts evaporation, moderates soil temperature, slows runoff, adds organic matter that raises water-holding capacity.

1 and 3 are the two pillars of conservation agriculture; 2 belongs to soil chemistry, not water budgeting. → **1 and 3 only**.
questions.tagging_note: Straddles agriculture practice (zero tillage, residue retention, irrigation water use -> GEO-17) and soil chemistry/degradation (gypsum on sodic soils -> GEO-15). A dedicated 'water resources / watershed and water conservation' topic does not exist in the vocabulary; GEO-17 only mentions irrigation in passing, so this is a partial fit rather than an exact one.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
The nation-wide 'Soil Health Card Scheme' aims at
1. expanding the cultivable area under irrigation.
2. enabling the banks to assess the quantum of loans to be granted to farmers on the basis of soil quality.
3. checking the overuse of fertilizers in farmlands.
Which of the above statements is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
Soil Health Card Scheme (launched **Feb 2015, Suratgarh, Rajasthan**) gives every farm holding a card every 2–3 years reporting **12 parameters** — N, P, K, S, the micronutrients (Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, B), plus pH, EC and organic carbon — with crop-wise fertiliser recommendations.

**1 — wrong.** Expanding irrigated area is **PMKSY** ('Har Khet Ko Pani'), a different scheme entirely. SHC does not create irrigation.

**2 — wrong.** Credit assessment runs on Kisan Credit Card / scale-of-finance norms. **The card carries no credit-linkage function** and banks are not a stakeholder in it.

**3 — correct.** The whole rationale is to correct the skewed NPK ratio and stop blanket urea overuse by telling the farmer what the soil actually lacks. → **3 only**.
questions.tagging_note: Scheme-based question: Soil Health Card sits under agriculture policy/subsidies (ECO-14) and the schemes tracker (CAI-10); statement 3 turns on fertilizer overuse and soil quality (GEO-15).

questions.stem:
Consider the following pairs :

| | *Commonly used / consumed materials* | *Unwanted or controversial chemicals likely to be found in them* |
|---|---|---|
| 1. | Lipstick | Lead |
| 2. | Soft drinks | Brominated vegetable oils |
| 3. | Chinese fast food | Monosodium glutamate |

Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched ?
questions.explanation_md:
**1. Lipstick — Lead: correct.** Lead occurs as a contaminant of the colour pigments; FDA and Indian CSE surveys have repeatedly found detectable lead in lipsticks. A neurotoxin with no safe threshold, hence the controversy.

**2. Soft drinks — Brominated vegetable oil: correct.** BVO is a **clouding/emulsifying agent used in citrus-flavoured sodas** to keep the flavour oils dispersed. Bromine accumulation concerns led to its removal by major brands and eventual bans.

**3. Chinese fast food — Monosodium glutamate: correct.** MSG (ajinomoto) is the umami flavour enhancer of Chinese/Indo-Chinese cooking; 'Chinese Restaurant Syndrome' is the classic controversy.

All three pairs hold. → **1, 2 and 3**
questions.tagging_note: Nothing in the vocabulary covers food safety, adulteration or FSSAI-style contaminant questions — this is a genuine gap in the syllabus tree. SNT-13 (everyday chemistry) is the nearest genuine fit; ENV-11 added only for the toxic-contaminant angle (lead). Format recorded as 'pairs' because it is a pair-matching item, though the stem asks which pairs are correct rather than how many.

questions.stem:
Organic Light Emitting Diodes (OLEDs) are used to create digital display in many devices. What are the advantages of OLED displays over Liquid Crystal displays ?
1. OLED displays can be fabricated on flexible plastic substrates.
2. Roll-up displays embedded in clothing can be made using OLEDs.
3. Transparent displays are possible using OLEDs.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
options: None of the above statements is correct
questions.explanation_md:
The deciding property: **an OLED pixel emits its own light, so no backlight, no polarisers and no rigid glass light-guide are needed** — that single fact makes all three statements follow.

**1 — correct.** The organic layers are thin films deposited at low temperature, so **flexible plastic (PET/polyimide) substrates** work; an LCD's backlight assembly and liquid-crystal cell need a rigid, flat panel.

**2 — correct.** Because the stack is thin and bendable, roll-up and wearable/clothing-embedded displays are a demonstrated OLED application.

**3 — correct.** With no backlight behind it, an OLED panel can be made **transparent** when its pixels are off — impossible for an LCD, which must sit in front of an opaque backlight.

→ **1, 2 and 3**
questions.tagging_note: Display technology is not named anywhere in the vocabulary. OLED as an organic-semiconductor material best fits SNT-11 (new materials); SNT-13 (everyday physics) is the fallback. Neither is a clean fit — a 'display and consumer electronics' slot is missing.

questions.stem:
Which of the following is/are famous for Sun temples ?
1. Arasavalli
2. Amarakantak
3. Omkareshwar
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**1. Arasavalli — correct.** In **Srikakulam district, Andhra Pradesh**, the Sri Suryanarayana Swamy temple — one of the very few functioning Sun temples in India, built by Kalinga ruler Devendra Varma; sunrays fall on the deity on specific days.

**2. Amarakantak — wrong.** In Anuppur district, MP, on the Maikal hills — the **source of the Narmada** (also Son and Johila). Its temples are Narmada/Shiva shrines, not solar.

**3. Omkareshwar — wrong.** An island in the Narmada in Khandwa district, MP — one of the **twelve Jyotirlingas**, i.e. a Shiva temple.

Sun temples worth remembering: Konark (Odisha), Modhera (Gujarat), Martand (Kashmir), Dakshinaark/Deo (Bihar), Arasavalli (AP). → **1 only**
questions.tagging_note: Primarily temple architecture and famous temples (ART-02). GEO-24 included because the discriminator is really place-location knowledge — Amarakantak and Omkareshwar are Narmada/Jyotirlinga sites, not Sun temples.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. In the election for Lok Sabha or State Assembly, the winning candidate must get at least 50 percent of the votes polled, to be declared elected.
2. According to the provisions laid down in the Constitution of India, in Lok Sabha, the Speaker's post goes to the majority party and the Deputy Speaker's to the Opposition.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**1 — wrong.** India uses **First-Past-The-Post (simple plurality)**: the candidate with the most votes wins, however small the share. No 50% threshold and no run-off. (A 50%+1 requirement exists only for the *Presidential* election, via the quota in the single transferable vote system.)

**2 — wrong.** **Article 93 says only that the House 'shall choose two members' as Speaker and Deputy Speaker** — it names no party. Giving the Deputy Speaker's post to the Opposition is a *convention*, and one that has been ignored (the 17th Lok Sabha had no Deputy Speaker at all).

Both statements attribute rules to the Constitution that it does not contain. → **Neither 1 nor 2**
questions.tagging_note: Two independent facts: statement 1 is the FPTP plurality system (POL-26, elections/RPA); statement 2 is the Speaker and Deputy Speaker (POL-18, Parliament). Primary set to POL-18 as the presiding-officer provision is the load-bearing half, but POL-26 is an equally genuine tag.

questions.stem:
Which of the following has/have occurred in India after its liberalization of economic policies in 1991 ?
1. Share of agriculture in GDP increased enormously.
2. Share of India's exports in world trade increased.
3. FDI inflows increased.
4. India's foreign exchange reserves increased enormously.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**1 — wrong, and it decides the question.** Agriculture's share of GDP has **fallen steadily since 1991 — roughly 29–30% then to under 18% now**. Its share of *employment* stayed stubbornly high; that gap is the standard 'structural retardation' point. Any option containing 1 is out, which kills (a) and (d).

**2 — correct.** India's share of world merchandise exports rose from about 0.5% in 1990–91 to roughly 1.7%+ today (services share far higher).

**3 — correct.** FDI was near-zero pre-1991 under the FERA regime; post-liberalisation it rose from a few hundred million dollars to tens of billions annually.

**4 — correct.** The classic contrast: forex reserves were about **$1 billion (two weeks of imports) in the 1991 crisis**, versus hundreds of billions today.

→ **2, 3 and 4 only**
questions.tagging_note: Three of the four statements are external sector (export share, FDI inflows, forex reserves -> ECO-12); statement 1 is sectoral composition of GDP (ECO-01). There is no dedicated '1991 reforms / LPG' topic in the vocabulary — ECO-19 covers planning, not liberalization history.
questions.transcription_note: Code line reads 'codes given below' (plural) as printed, unlike the singular 'code' used elsewhere on this page.

questions.stem: What is the application of Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer Technology ?
options: Production of organisms free of diseases
questions.explanation_md:
**SCNT = the Dolly technique.** The nucleus of a **somatic (body) cell** is transferred into an **enucleated egg cell**; the egg reprogrammes that nucleus, the embryo is implanted in a surrogate, and the offspring is a genetic copy of the somatic-cell donor. Dolly the sheep (1996) and India's cloned buffalo *Garima* (NDRI Karnal) are the standard examples.

So the application is **reproductive cloning of animals**. (The same technique used to derive stem-cell lines rather than a live birth is called *therapeutic* cloning.)

Why the others fail: biolarvicides come from *Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis*/*B. sphaericus*; biodegradable plastics (PHB/PLA) from microbial fermentation; disease-free plants come from **meristem tissue culture**, not SCNT.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) helps in promoting the financial inclusion in the country.
2. NPCI has launched RuPay, a card payment scheme.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**1 — correct.** NPCI is the umbrella retail-payments organisation set up in 2008 by **RBI and IBA** under Section 25 of the Companies Act (a 'not for profit' company). Its products — **AePS, NACH, IMPS, UPI, BHIM, ***99# USSD** — are explicitly built to extend payments to low-income and rural users, so promoting financial inclusion is a stated objective.

**2 — correct.** NPCI launched **RuPay in 2012**, India's domestic card payment network, as an alternative to Visa/Mastercard with lower transaction costs; it is the card issued under Jan Dhan accounts.

Both statements stand. → **Both 1 and 2**
questions.tagging_note: NPCI is named only obliquely in the vocabulary — ECO-20 lists UPI (an NPCI product) and is the closest home for retail payment infrastructure; ECO-06 carries financial inclusion and ECO-04 the payments-bank/banking-structure angle. A distinct 'payment systems' topic does not exist.

questions.stem: The term 'M-STrIPES' is sometimes seen in the news in the context of
questions.explanation_md:
**M-STrIPES = Monitoring System for Tigers – Intensive Protection and Ecological Status.** A software/GPS-based patrol and monitoring tool developed by the **National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) with the Wildlife Institute of India**.

Forest guards on foot patrol log GPS tracks, signs of tigers and prey, carcasses and evidence of poaching on handheld devices/an app; the data feed a GIS system that maps patrol coverage and threat hotspots. It is also used in the four-yearly **All India Tiger Estimation**.

So the context is **maintenance/management of tiger reserves**. (Not to be confused with **NavIC/IRNSS**, the indigenous satellite navigation system.)
questions.tagging_note: M-STrIPES is the NTCA tiger-reserve monitoring protocol — Project Tiger (ENV-08), applied inside protected areas (ENV-06).

questions.stem:
What is/are the most likely advantages of implementing 'Goods and Services Tax (GST)' ?
1. It will replace multiple taxes collected by multiple authorities and will thus create a single market in India.
2. It will drastically reduce the 'Current Account Deficit' of India and will enable it to increase its foreign exchange reserves.
3. It will enormously increase the growth and size of economy of India and will enable it to overtake China in the near future.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**Only statement 1 is a genuine, direct advantage of GST.**

- **St. 1 — correct.** GST subsumed excise, service tax, VAT, CST, octroi, entry tax etc., levied by Centre and States separately. One destination-based tax with seamless input tax credit removes inter-state tax barriers → **"one nation, one tax, one market."**
- **St. 2 — wrong.** GST is a *domestic indirect tax*. Exports are zero-rated and imports pay IGST, so it is broadly neutral on trade. CAD is driven by oil prices, gold imports and export competitiveness — not by how India taxes internal supply. "Drastically reduce CAD" is unsupportable.
- **St. 3 — wrong.** Estimates put the GST growth boost at roughly 1–2 percentage points of GDP, not "enormous." India's GDP was about one-fifth of China's in 2017; no indirect tax reform overtakes that "in the near future."

**Exam tip:** words like *drastically*, *enormously*, *overtake China* are almost always the examiner marking a statement as false. Answer: **1 only.**

questions.stem: 'Broad-based Trade and Investment Agreement (BTIA)' is sometimes seen in the news in the context of negotiations held between India and
options: Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development
questions.explanation_md:
**BTIA is the India–EU free trade agreement**, under negotiation since **June 2007**.

- Formally the *Bilateral Trade and Investment Agreement* / *Broad-based Trade and Investment Agreement* between **India and the European Union**.
- Talks stalled in 2013 over sticking points: EU wanted lower tariffs on **automobiles, wines and spirits** and stronger IPR/data-exclusivity; India wanted **"data secure nation" status** and easier **Mode 4** (movement of professionals).
- Relaunched in 2022; the EU is one of India's largest trading partners.

GCC talks are a separate FTA; OECD and SCO are not trade-agreement negotiating partners of this kind. **The EU is the only body India negotiates a "broad-based" trade *and investment* pact with.**
questions.tagging_note: BTIA is the India-EU FTA under negotiation: sits on CAI-06 (FTAs) and CAI-02 (India and the EU).

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. India has ratified the Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA) of WTO.
2. TFA is a part of WTO's Bali Ministerial Package of 2013.
3. TFA came into force in January 2016.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Statements 1 and 2 correct; 3 wrong on the date.**

- **St. 1 — correct.** India **ratified the TFA in April 2016**, after the Nov 2014 India–US deal that linked TFA acceptance to a permanent solution on **public stockholding for food security** (the Bali "peace clause" made indefinite).
- **St. 2 — correct.** TFA was the centrepiece of the **Bali Ministerial Package, WTO's 9th Ministerial Conference, December 2013** — the first multilateral agreement concluded since the WTO was formed in 1995.
- **St. 3 — wrong.** **TFA entered into force on 22 February 2017**, the day two-thirds of members (112) had ratified — not January 2016.

TFA covers customs simplification, transparency and expedited release of goods. Answer: **1 and 2 only.**
questions.tagging_note: WTO Bali package / TFA — ECO-13 covers WTO as an institution; CAI-06 covers the trade-diplomacy angle.

questions.stem: What is the importance of developing Chabahar Port by India ?
options: India's trade with African countries will enormously increase.
India's relations with oil-producing Arab countries will be strengthened.
India will not depend on Pakistan for access to Afghanistan and Central Asia.
Pakistan will facilitate and protect the installation of a gas pipeline between Iraq and India.
questions.explanation_md:
**Chabahar bypasses Pakistan.**

Pakistan denies India overland transit rights, so Indian goods cannot reach Afghanistan or Central Asia by road. Chabahar, on Iran's **Sistan-Baluchistan coast on the Gulf of Oman (outside the Strait of Hormuz)**, gives India a sea route to Iran and then road/rail onward — the **Zaranj–Delaram highway** built by India links to Afghanistan's Garland Ring Road, and the port feeds into the **International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC)** toward Central Asia and Russia.

The 2016 trilateral India–Iran–Afghanistan agreement covers **Shahid Beheshti terminal**. It is also India's strategic answer to China's **Gwadar** in Pakistan, ~170 km away.

Other options fail: it is not an Africa route, Iran is not an Arab state, and Pakistan protecting an Iraq–India pipeline is fiction. **Answer: c.**
questions.tagging_note: Chabahar straddles three CAI topics — connectivity project (CAI-06), India-Iran/Central Asia (CAI-03), and access to Afghanistan bypassing Pakistan (CAI-01). No single topic owns port/connectivity projects, so CAI-06 was chosen as the literal 'connectivity projects' fit.

questions.stem:
In India, it is legally mandatory for which of the following to report on cyber security incidents ?
1. Service providers
2. Data centres
3. Body corporate
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**All three are legally bound to report cyber security incidents to CERT-In.**

Under **Section 70B of the IT Act, 2000** and the **Information Technology (CERT-In) Rules, 2013**, Rule 12(1)(a) makes it **mandatory** for *service providers, intermediaries, data centres and body corporate* to report specified cyber security incidents to **CERT-In** — the national nodal agency — within a reasonable time.

So:
- **St. 1 Service providers — yes**
- **St. 2 Data centres — yes**
- **St. 3 Body corporate — yes**

(Section 43A separately imposes compensation liability on a *body corporate* handling sensitive personal data.) Answer: **1, 2 and 3.**
questions.tagging_note: Tests CERT-In / IT Act mandatory incident reporting — falls squarely in SNT-10 cybersecurity, though the vocabulary has no dedicated IT-law topic.

questions.stem: Right to vote and to be elected in India is a
questions.explanation_md:
**The option set is a hierarchy-of-source question, not a case-law question.** UPSC is asking *where does this right come from*: Part III (Fundamental) → elsewhere in the Constitution (Constitutional) → an ordinary statute (Legal). Both halves of the compound right — "to vote" **and** "to be elected" — are written into the Constitution itself.

- **To vote — Article 326.** Elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies "shall be on the basis of adult suffrage": every citizen not below 18 and not otherwise disqualified *shall be entitled* to be registered as a voter. Article 325 adds that no one may be excluded on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex.
- **To be elected — Articles 84 and 173** fix the qualifications for Parliament and State legislatures; **Articles 102 and 191** fix the disqualifications.
- The Representation of the People Act, 1951 (s. 62 for voting, ss. 3–5 for candidature) only **implements** what those Articles already command. It is machinery, not source.

**Why (d) Legal Right is the trap.** The phrase "pure and simple, a statutory right" comes from *N.P. Ponnuswami* (1952), *Jyoti Basu v. Debi Ghosal* (1982) and *Kuldip Nayar* (2006) — a real and genuinely contested line. But two things sink it here:

1. **"Legal right" in this option set means a right created by ordinary law, removable by a simple majority.** The franchise is not. Lowering the voting age from 21 to 18 required the **61st Constitutional Amendment, 1988** — Parliament could not do it by amending the RPA. If a constitutional amendment is needed to change the right, the right lives in the Constitution. That single fact settles the classification.
2. That case law is about the **exercise and enforcement** of the vote inside an election dispute — no election petition lies except as the statute provides. *Kuldip Nayar* in particular concerned Rajya Sabha voting, an **indirect** election under Art. 80(4), where Art. 326 adult suffrage does not even apply.

**Why the others fail.**

- **(a) Fundamental Right** — not in Part III, so no Article 32 remedy; enforcement is under Article 226. *PUCL* (2003) read the voter's *right to know* a candidate's antecedents into Art. 19(1)(a); it never made the franchise itself a fundamental right.
- **(b) Natural Right** — natural rights inhere in a person as a human being, prior to the State. The franchise is conferred by a polity on **citizens** who clear age and qualification tests; foreigners, minors and disqualified persons do not hold it.

**Exam rule to carry forward:** when UPSC offers Fundamental / Constitutional / Legal for something that sits in the Constitution but outside Part III, the answer is **Constitutional Right** — the same bucket as Art. 265 (no tax without authority of law), Art. 300A (property) and Art. 301 (freedom of trade).
questions.tagging_note: Right to vote sits under elections/RPA (POL-26); the distractor set turns on the Fundamental Right vs constitutional right distinction (POL-07).
questions.review_flag: Official key says c, worked solution said d (medium confidence).

questions.stem: What is the purpose of 'evolved Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (eLISA)' project ?
options: To detect the effectiveness of missile defence system
To study the effect of solar flares on our communication systems
questions.explanation_md:
**eLISA is a space-based gravitational wave detector.**

The **evolved Laser Interferometer Space Antenna**, an **ESA-led mission (with NASA)**, will fly **three spacecraft in a triangular formation millions of km apart**, using laser interferometry to detect the tiny spacetime ripples of **gravitational waves**.

Being in space, it detects **low-frequency** waves (supermassive black hole mergers) that ground detectors like **LIGO** cannot — LIGO's 4 km arms only reach higher frequencies. The **LISA Pathfinder** (launched Dec 2015) successfully tested the technology.

Gravitational waves were predicted by **Einstein's General Relativity (1915)** and first directly detected by **LIGO in Sept 2015, announced 11 Feb 2016** — which is why this was in the news for Prelims 2017. India's contribution is **LIGO-India** in Maharashtra. Answer: **b.**

questions.stem:
What is the purpose of 'Vidyanjali Yojana' ?
1. To enable the famous foreign educational institutions to open their campuses in India.
2. To increase the quality of education provided in government schools by taking help from the private sector and the community.
3. To encourage voluntary monetary contributions from private individuals and organizations so as to improve the infrastructure facilities for primary and secondary schools.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**Only statement 2 is correct.**

**Vidyanjali** is a **school volunteer programme launched by MHRD in June 2016** under *Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan*, enabling volunteers — NRIs, retired teachers, professionals, private-sector employees, students — to **contribute their time and skills in government schools** for co-scholastic activities (reading, storytelling, arts, sports, spoken English), *not* to replace regular teaching.

- **St. 1 — wrong.** Foreign university campuses in India is an entirely separate policy question, nothing to do with Vidyanjali.
- **St. 2 — correct.** Improving quality in government schools through private-sector and community help is precisely its aim.
- **St. 3 — wrong at the time.** The original scheme sought **volunteer service, not monetary contributions or infrastructure funding**. (The later *Vidyanjali 2.0*, 2021, did add asset/material donation — but that is after this paper.)

Answer: **2 only.**

questions.stem: What is the aim of the programme 'Unnat Bharat Abhiyan' ?
options: Achieving 100% literacy by promoting collaboration between voluntary organizations and government's education system and local communities.
Connecting institutions of higher education with local communities to address development challenges through appropriate technologies.
Strengthening India's scientific research institutions in order to make India a scientific and technological power.
Developing human capital by allocating special funds for health care and education of rural and urban poor, and organizing skill development programmes and vocational training for them.
questions.explanation_md:
**Unnat Bharat Abhiyan links higher education institutions to villages.**

Launched by **MHRD in November 2014, coordinated by IIT Delhi**, its aim is to connect **institutions of higher education (IITs, NITs, universities, colleges) with local rural communities** — each institution adopts a **cluster of villages** — to address their development challenges using **appropriate/sustainable technology**.

The tagline is *"Transformational change in rural development processes by leveraging knowledge institutions."* Focus areas include sustainable agriculture, water management, renewable energy, artisan livelihoods and basic rural infrastructure. **UBA 2.0 (2018)** made participation subject-based and selective.

Distractors: 100% literacy is not its aim; strengthening research institutions is DST's domain; the last option describes a generic poverty/skilling scheme. **The word "appropriate technologies" + "local communities" is the signature of UBA.** Answer: **b.**

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. The Election Commission of India is a five-member body.
2. Union Ministry of Home Affairs decides the election schedule for the conduct of both general elections and bye-elections.
3. Election Commission resolves the disputes relating to splits/mergers of recognised political parties.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Only statement 3 is correct.**

- **St. 1 — wrong.** The ECI is **not fixed at five members**. **Article 324(2)**: the Commission consists of the CEC and *such number of other Election Commissioners as the President may from time to time fix*. It was a single-member body till 1989, briefly three, single again, and **three-member since 1 October 1993** (CEC + 2 ECs). Decisions are by majority.
- **St. 2 — wrong.** The **Election Commission**, not the Home Ministry, announces the election schedule. The whole point of Art. 324 is that *superintendence, direction and control* of elections rests with an **independent** body, insulated from the executive.
- **St. 3 — correct.** Under **Para 15 of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968**, the ECI decides disputes among **rival factions of a recognised political party** on splits and mergers, and allots the party name and symbol (e.g. Samajwadi Party 2017, AIADMK).

Answer: **3 only.**
questions.tagging_note: ECI composition and powers (POL-24); statement 3 on splits/mergers of recognised parties also touches POL-26.

questions.stem: In India, if a species of tortoise is declared protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, what does it imply ?
options: It enjoys the same level of protection as the tiger.
It no longer exists in the wild, a few individuals are under captive protection; and now it is impossible to prevent its extinction.
It is endemic to a particular region of India.
Both (b) and (c) stated above are correct in this context.
questions.explanation_md:
**Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 is the highest protection category — the tiger is also Schedule I, so anything placed there gets the same legal protection.**

Why the others fail:
- **(b)** wrong — Schedule I listing says nothing about being extinct in the wild. Many Schedule I species (tiger, elephant, gharial) have healthy or recovering wild populations.
- **(c)** wrong — Schedule I is not about endemism. Migratory and widely distributed species are also listed.

Key point: penalties for Schedule I offences are the most severe (imprisonment plus fine), and hunting is barred except in narrow circumstances with Chief Wildlife Warden permission.

questions.stem: In India, Judicial Review implies
options: the power of the Judiciary to pronounce upon the constitutionality of laws and executive orders.
the power of the Judiciary to question the wisdom of the laws enacted by the Legislatures.
the power of the Judiciary to review all the legislative enactments before they are assented to by the President.
the power of the Judiciary to review its own judgements given earlier in similar or different cases.
questions.explanation_md:
**Judicial review = the power of courts to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders, and declare them void if they violate the Constitution.**

Ruling out the rest:
- **(b)** courts judge *legality*, not the *wisdom* or policy merit of a law — that is the legislature's domain.
- **(c)** India has no system of *pre-enactment* judicial scrutiny (that is French-style *a priori* review). The one narrow exception is the President's advisory reference under **Art. 143**, which is discretionary, not routine.
- **(d)** that is the **review jurisdiction** under Art. 137 (Supreme Court reviewing its own judgments) — a different concept entirely.

Basis: Arts. 13, 32, 131–136, 143, 226, 246.

questions.stem:
With reference to Indian freedom struggle, consider the following events :
1. Mutiny in Royal Indian Navy
2. Quit India Movement launched
3. Second Round Table Conference
What is the correct chronological sequence of the above events ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Second RTC (1931) → Quit India (1942) → RIN Mutiny (1946). So 3-2-1.**

- **Second Round Table Conference — Sept–Dec 1931**, London. Gandhi attended as sole Congress representative under the Gandhi–Irwin Pact; it collapsed over the communal question.
- **Quit India Movement — 8 August 1942**, Bombay AICC session, "Do or Die".
- **Royal Indian Navy Mutiny — 18–23 February 1946**, began on HMIS *Talwar* in Bombay; Sardar Patel and Jinnah persuaded the ratings to surrender.

Memory hook: the RIN Mutiny is the *last* major pre-Independence uprising — anything before 1947 in a sequence question almost always ends with it.
questions.tagging_note: Chronology question: numbered events (RIN Mutiny 1946, Quit India 1942, Second RTC 1931) with orderings as options. The vocabulary has no 'sequence' format, so 'simple' is the least-wrong fit — the options are plain orderings, not statement-truth codes. Content straddles HIS-13 (Quit India, INA, RIN Mutiny) and HIS-11 (Round Table Conferences).

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. Tax revenue as a percent of GDP of India has steadily increased in the last decade.
2. Fiscal deficit as a percent of GDP of India has steadily increased in the last decade.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Neither statement is correct — the word that kills both is "steadily".**

- **St. 1 — wrong.** Tax-to-GDP ratio did not rise steadily over the decade to 2016-17. Gross tax revenue was ~11.9% of GDP in 2007-08, fell to ~9.6-10% around 2009-10 after the crisis-era stimulus and excise/service tax cuts, then climbed back to ~11% only later. A fall then a rise is not "steady increase".
- **St. 2 — wrong, and in fact the trend is the opposite.** Fiscal deficit spiked to **6.5% of GDP in 2009-10**, then was pulled *down* under FRBM consolidation to ~4.5% (2013-14), 3.9% (2015-16) and 3.5% (2016-17). Clearly declining, not increasing.

Exam rule: statements containing *steadily / continuously / consistently* about Indian macro data are almost always false, because 2008-09 breaks nearly every trend line.

questions.stem: Recently there was a proposal to translocate some of the lions from their natural habitat in Gujarat to which one of the following sites ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Kuno–Palpur Wildlife Sanctuary, Sheopur district, Madhya Pradesh** — the designated second home for the Asiatic lion.

- Gir (Gujarat) holds the world's only wild Asiatic lion population; a single epidemic or fire could wipe it out, hence the need for a second site.
- The **Supreme Court ordered the translocation in April 2013**, giving MoEF six months; Gujarat has resisted implementation ever since.
- Kuno villages were relocated in the 1990s specifically to prepare the habitat.

Note for updating: Kuno was later (2022) used instead for the **African cheetah introduction** — but the lion translocation order is what this question tests. Sariska and Corbett are tiger reserves; Mudumalai is in the Nilgiris.
questions.tagging_note: Asiatic Lion translocation to Kuno — sits between ENV-08 (species conservation projects) and ENV-06 (protected-area names/locations). ENV-08 chosen as primary since the trigger is the reintroduction project, not the sanctuary category.

questions.stem:
Which of the following are **not** necessarily the consequences of the proclamation of the President's rule in a State ?
1. Dissolution of the State Legislative Assembly
2. Removal of the Council of Ministers in the State
3. Dissolution of the local bodies
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**Under Article 356, only the removal of the State Council of Ministers is automatic. The other two are not necessary consequences — so 1 and 3.**

- **1. Dissolution of the Assembly — NOT necessary.** The President *may* dissolve the Assembly, but usually keeps it in **suspended animation** so it can be revived. *S.R. Bommai (1994)* held the Assembly cannot be dissolved before Parliament approves the proclamation.
- **2. Removal of the Council of Ministers — this IS a necessary consequence.** The President assumes the functions of the State government, so the CM and ministry go automatically.
- **3. Dissolution of local bodies — NOT a consequence at all.** Panchayats and municipalities are separate constitutional bodies (Parts IX and IXA) with their own five-year terms; President's rule does not touch them.

The question asks for what is *not necessarily* a consequence → 1 and 3.
questions.tagging_note: Core is Art 356 consequences (POL-16); statement 3 on dissolution of local bodies touches POL-22.
questions.transcription_note: In the printed paper 'not' is set in bold italic.

questions.stem:
Which of the following are envisaged by the Right against Exploitation in the Constitution of India ?
1. Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour
2. Abolition of untouchability
3. Protection of the interests of minorities
4. Prohibition of employment of children in factories and mines
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
questions.explanation_md:
**Right against Exploitation = Articles 23 and 24 only. So 1 and 4.**

- **1. Traffic in human beings and forced labour (begar) — YES, Article 23.**
- **2. Abolition of untouchability — NO.** That is **Article 17**, under the *Right to Equality*.
- **3. Protection of interests of minorities — NO.** That is **Articles 29–30**, *Cultural and Educational Rights*.
- **4. Prohibition of employment of children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work — YES, Article 24.**

Remember the pairing: **Right against Exploitation contains exactly two articles, 23 and 24 — trafficking/forced labour and child labour.**
questions.tagging_note: Right against Exploitation (Art 23–24) is POL-09; the distractors pull in untouchability/Art 17 (POL-07) and minority interests/Art 29–30 (POL-10).

questions.stem: Which of the following is geographically closest to Great Nicobar ?
questions.explanation_md:
**Sumatra (Indonesia) — Indira Point on Great Nicobar is only about 150 km from Banda Aceh in northern Sumatra**, across the Great Channel (Six Degree Channel).

- **Indira Point** is India's southernmost land point, ~6°45′N.
- The **Six Degree Channel** separates Great Nicobar from Sumatra — the narrowest India–Indonesia gap, which is why India and Indonesia hold coordinated **IND-INDO CORPAT** patrols there.
- Java and Borneo lie much further south-east; Sri Lanka is roughly 1,200+ km west across the Bay of Bengal.

Also fix the other channel: **Ten Degree Channel** separates Little Andaman from Car Nicobar (Andamans from Nicobars).

questions.stem: Out of the following statements, choose the one that brings out the principle underlying the Cabinet form of Government :
options: An arrangement for minimizing the criticism against the Government whose responsibilities are complex and hard to carry out to the satisfaction of all.
A mechanism for speeding up the activities of the Government whose responsibilities are increasing day by day.
A mechanism of parliamentary democracy for ensuring collective responsibility of the Government to the people.
A device for strengthening the hands of the head of the Government whose hold over the people is in a state of decline.
questions.explanation_md:
**The Cabinet system rests on collective responsibility — Article 75(3): the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, and through it to the people.**

- Ministers swim or sink together; a vote of no-confidence against one minister brings down the whole ministry.
- Cabinet decisions bind every minister, whatever their private view — a minister who cannot defend a decision must resign.

Why the others fail: **(a)** and **(d)** treat the Cabinet as a political shield for the government or the PM, not a constitutional principle; **(b)** administrative speed is at best a by-product, not the underlying principle. Only (c) names the actual doctrine.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is **not** a feature of Indian federalism ?
options: There is an independent judiciary in India.
Powers have been clearly divided between the Centre and the States.
The federating units have been given unequal representation in the Rajya Sabha.
It is the result of an agreement among the federating units.
questions.explanation_md:
**Indian federalism is NOT the result of an agreement among federating units — it was created by devolution from a unitary British Indian centre.**

- The states did **not** come together voluntarily like the American colonies. Article 1 calls India a **"Union of States"** — Ambedkar explained the phrase was chosen precisely because the Union is **not the result of an agreement**, and no state has the right to secede.
- Contrast: the USA is a "coming together" federation; India is a **"holding together"** federation, with states created and reorganised by Parliament under **Article 3**.

The other three ARE features: an **integrated independent judiciary**, a clear **division of powers via the Seventh Schedule** (Union, State, Concurrent Lists), and **unequal Rajya Sabha representation** based on population (unlike the US Senate's equal two-per-state) — the last is an Indian deviation from classical federalism but is genuinely a feature of the system.
questions.tagging_note: Features of Indian federalism sit in POL-14 (Parliamentary & Federal System); the Centre–State division-of-powers option also touches POL-15.
